questions.question: A policy adviser at a Brazilian securities regulator is drafting a gap analysis against the key focus areas that standard-setting bodies have set out in responding to AI applications. Each of the following names focus areas on that list EXCEPT:

options.text: Governance of AI use, and transparency and explainability.
Outsourcing practices, and data quality and bias.
Reporting requirements, and maintaining meaningful human oversight.
Presuming outsourced AI riskier, and ending human oversight.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The six focus areas**

Governance of AI use; transparency and explainability; outsourcing practices; data quality and bias; reporting requirements; maintaining meaningful human oversight.

**Step 2 – Find the option that is not on the list**

A, B and C between them name all six. D pairs two positions the reading rejects: there is no indication that outsourced models are riskier than internally developed ones, and maintaining meaningful human oversight is itself a focus area (Schweser Module Quiz 100.3, Question 1, wrong options C and A).

⇒ D is the exception.

**Interpretation**

Outsourcing is a focus because institutions stay fully responsible for what they buy, not because bought models are presumed worse, and human oversight is to be maintained, not phased out. The risk the reading does attach to outsourcing is concentration: reliance on a few third-party providers (CI-1 c).

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d, Module Quiz 100.3 Q1

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.2)

a.reason: On the list: governance of AI use, and transparency and explainability, are both focus areas.

b.reason: On the list: outsourcing practices, and data quality and bias.

c.reason: On the list: reporting requirements, and meaningful human oversight.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a Mumbai brokerage is drafting a slide that attributes AI-related regulatory work to the bodies named in the IMF reading. Which attribution is correct?

options.text: The Basel Committee introduced a new AI framework in 2024, building on the FSB’s work on the volatility linked to algorithmic trading.
IOSCO has focused on volatility linked to algorithmic trading and on AI-related risks in market intermediation and asset management.
The FSB has led the work on AI risks in market intermediation and asset management, while IOSCO concentrates on bank capital standards.
National governments’ AI strategies concentrate on capital markets conduct, leaving cybercrime prevention and data protection to IOSCO.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The bodies named**

The FSB, BCBS, BIS, NIST, IOSCO and national regulators have acted to strengthen investor protection, market integrity and financial stability, building on existing frameworks and in some cases introducing new ones.

**Step 2 – Attach each initiative to its body**

NIST: the 2024 AI framework. IOSCO: market volatility associated with algorithmic trading, and AI-related risks in market intermediation and asset management. Governments: broader AI strategies on cybercrime prevention, data protection and sound AI governance.

⇒ Only B attributes correctly.

**Interpretation**

Governance questions are won on who. IOSCO, the BCBS and the BIS reappear together as the source of the margin proposals in the first policy priority.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q33 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.3)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the 2024 AI framework is NIST’s, and the algorithmic trading work is IOSCO’s.

c.reason: Role misassignment: the intermediation and asset management workstream is IOSCO’s; nothing in the reading gives IOSCO a bank capital role.

d.reason: Role misassignment and scope error: cybercrime prevention and data protection are what government AI strategies emphasise.

questions.question: A financial stability directorate at the central bank of Chile is drafting a roadmap to support the safe adoption of AI in capital markets. Which step is most consistent with the IMF reading’s recommendations?

options.text: Assess whether existing frameworks adequately address robustness, explainability, cybersecurity, and data bias and privacy.
Replace existing regulatory frameworks with AI-specific rulebooks, since current frameworks were not designed with AI in mind.
Develop AI governance principles within the authority alone, to keep them independent of the industry they will govern.
Leave explainability out of the framework review, because it is a design choice that each firm makes model by model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three recommendations**

Evaluate the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks; develop new risk management frameworks; advance principles for AI governance through public-private collaboration.

**Step 2 – What the review must test**

Whether the current frameworks suﬀiciently address robustness, explainability, cybersecurity, and data bias and privacy.

⇒ A is the first recommendation with its stated test.

**Interpretation**

The approach is to build on what exists, add where needed and write governance principles with the industry. That matches the survey respondents’ preference for best practices and flexible guidelines (CI-1 c).

questions.question: The head of SupTech at a supervisory authority in Kenya wants AI to help modernise the authority’s legacy surveillance code and to retrieve information faster from its archives. Which statement is consistent with the IMF reading?

options.text: These are RegTech uses, which the IMF assigns to regulated banks for their own compliance management rather than to the supervisors.
These are GenAI capabilities in the IMF reading, over and above automated data quality checks, data integration and anomaly detection.
These are the core supervisory gains from AI in general, while GenAI’s added value for supervisors lies in real-time market monitoring.
These uses fall outside supervision, since the IMF sees the value of AI for supervisors only in detecting anomalies in trading patterns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – General AI for supervisors**

Eﬀiciency gains through automated data quality checks, integration of multiple data sources and detection of trading pattern anomalies, plus real-time market monitoring and identification of misleading information.

**Step 2 – What GenAI adds**

Legacy code optimisation, content creation, improved information retrieval, and advanced code generation, debugging and explanation.

⇒ Modernising legacy code and faster retrieval are on the GenAI list.

**Interpretation**

This is the “tool” half of the LO. The “rule” half, policy on AI used by banks and NBFIs, is the four priorities.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.a and 100.d

a.reason: Role misassignment: RegTech is the banks’ compliance tooling; legacy code optimisation and retrieval are named among supervisors’ GenAI gains.

c.reason: Tier swap: real-time market monitoring is a general AI gain; legacy code and retrieval are the GenAI additions.

d.reason: Absolute claim: anomaly detection is one of several supervisory gains, alongside data checks, data integration, real-time monitoring and the GenAI uses.

A markets authority in Hong Kong is updating its response plan for dislocations caused by AI-driven trading, drawing on proposals from IOSCO, the Basel Committee and the BIS. Which review plan is most consistent with the IMF reading?

options.text: Review initial margin levels in normal conditions, and margin call volatility, variation margin flows and CCP model responsiveness under stress.
Review margin call volatility and variation margin flows in normal conditions, and initial margin levels and CCP margin models during stress.
Review maintenance margin minimums in normal conditions, and test algorithms only in controlled environments to avoid destabilising live markets.
Fix initial and variation margin at permanent levels, so that margin calls no longer change during the large price swings of a dislocation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The volatility toolkit**

Authorities should assess the quality of circuit breakers, test algorithms in controlled and stressed environments, and evaluate margin requirements and other buffers during large price swings.

**Step 2 – The margin agenda and its timing**

Based on IOSCO, BCBS and BIS proposals: review initial margin levels during normal conditions; review margin call volatility, variation margin collections and distributions, and the responsiveness of CCP margin models during market stress.

⇒ Set the baseline in calm conditions; watch the flows in the storm.

**Interpretation**

Initial margin is the buffer posted before stress arrives, which is why it is reviewed in normal times. The class notes run the four items together; the correction box restores the timing.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d, Module Quiz 100.3 Q2

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q35 and Q36 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (correction (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.6)

b.reason: Timing swap: initial margin is the normal-conditions item; margin call volatility and variation margin are stress-period items.

c.reason: Wrong input and dropped condition: maintenance margin is not on the agenda, and algorithms are tested in stressed as well as controlled environments.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the reading asks authorities to evaluate the adequacy and responsiveness of margins, not to freeze them.

questions.question: A supervisor at the Monetary Authority of Singapore is assigning the mapping tasks that the IMF recommends for AI-related risks. Which allocation is consistent with the reading?

options.text: Institutions map the links between critical IT infrastructure providers and major AI providers; authorities map each firm’s AI models and data.
Authorities map both sets of links, because institutions cannot see their own dependencies on third-party AI service providers.
Institutions map both sets of links, because the authorities’ role in the reading is limited to circuit breakers and margin rules.
Authorities map links between critical IT providers and major AI providers; institutions map their own AI models, data and infrastructure.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The authorities’ map**

Under the third-party priority, financial sector authorities should map the interconnections between critical IT infrastructure providers and major AI service providers, since disruption at these entities could have widespread consequences.

**Step 2 – The institutions’ map**

Under the opacity priority, financial institutions should be required to map interdependencies among their AI models, data sources and underlying technological infrastructure.

⇒ The system-wide map belongs to the authority; the firm-level map belongs to the firm.

**Interpretation**

The split mirrors the LO: what authorities do themselves, and what policy requires of regulated entities. A firm’s map also has to flag data that miss a full financial cycle or depend on a few external providers.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.7)

a.reason: Role misassignment: it swaps the two maps between authorities and institutions.

b.reason: Role misassignment: institutions are required to map their own interdependencies.

c.reason: Role misassignment and scope error: authorities map provider interconnections, and their priorities go well beyond circuit breakers and margins.

questions.question: A regulator in Ireland is designing measures to address the opacity and monitoring challenges that come with AI adoption by NBFIs. Which measure is most consistent with the IMF reading?

options.text: Exempt large traders from additional monitoring, since AI spreads trading activity across many smaller and more agile participants.
Accept training data drawn from the latest expansion only, since data from earlier cycles reflect an outdated structure of the market.
Require NBFIs to identify themselves and disclose AI-related information, and strengthen their liquidity buffers and risk management.
Limit the new disclosure requirements to banks, since NBFIs operate outside the perimeter of capital markets regulation and supervision.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Disclosure**

NBFIs should be required to identify themselves and disclose AI-related information.

**Step 2 – Resilience**

Strengthening liquidity buffers and enhancing risk management could improve NBFI resilience, mitigating the risk of liquidity runs and asset mispricing.

⇒ C states both halves of the NBFI response.

**Interpretation**

The measure answers the opacity challenge in CI-1 c: activity is moving to NBFIs that are lightly overseen compared with banks.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.c and 100.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q38 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip: large traders have always been a regulatory focus, and their importance increases in an AI-driven landscape.

b.reason: Polarity flip: risks arise precisely when data fail to capture a full financial cycle.

d.reason: Role misassignment: NBFIs are the target of the disclosure requirement, because that is where transparency is falling.

questions.question: As AI use expands, a securities authority in South Korea is reviewing options to maintain the integrity, eﬀiciency and resilience of over-the-counter (OTC) markets. Which package is most consistent with the IMF reading?

options.text: Scale back the collection of OTC transaction data to cut compliance costs, and restrict market makers’ liquidity provision during stress.
Require detailed OTC transaction data to be collected and disseminated, and develop liquidity and funding backstops for extreme stress.
Remove backstop liquidity and funding measures to avoid moral hazard, and rely on central clearing alone to absorb any extreme stress.
Exempt non-centrally cleared derivatives from margin requirements, so that incentives for central clearing are no longer needed.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Data**

Authorities could require the collection and dissemination of detailed information on OTC transactions by market participants.

**Step 2 – The policy menu**

Adjust liquidity frameworks; expand incentives for central clearing; enhance liquidity provision by market makers; introduce margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives; develop backstop measures for liquidity and funding in extreme stress.

⇒ B pairs the data requirement with the backstops.

**Interpretation**

Every item on the OTC menu moves in one direction: more information, more clearing, more liquidity, more margin, and a backstop for the extreme case.

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d

CI-2 • The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (FSB, November 2024) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q39 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 100.d; CI notes CI-1 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-1 d.9)

a.reason: Polarity flip on both halves: the reading would expand OTC data collection and enhance market makers’ liquidity provision.

c.reason: Polarity flip: backstops are to be developed, and central clearing incentives are one tool among several, not the only one.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the option is to introduce margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, alongside more incentives for central clearing.

questions.loText: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demandside drivers.
questions.reading: CI-2: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.topic: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q41 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a
questions.question: The head of digital strategy at a Canadian bank is drafting a board paper that uses the FSB’s framework to explain why AI adoption in financial services has accelerated since 2017. Which of the following classifications should the paper use?

options.text: Wider reliance on cloud providers and pre-trained models is a demand-side driver, because it reflects what institutions want to buy from vendors.
Pressure to keep pace with peers that are deploying GenAI is a supply-side driver, because it changes the AI tools that vendors bring to market.
Unstructured data growth is a supply-side driver because AI can combine it with quantitative data; eﬀicient compliance is a demand-side driver.
The Transformer architecture and cheaper GPU computing are demand-side drivers, because they raise the expected profitability of AI projects.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Sort by what the driver is**

Supply side: technological, data-related and business model developments. Demand side: profitability, competition and regulation.

⇒ Supply-side factors are capabilities; demand-side factors are motives.

**Step 2 – Place the two items in C**

The rapid growth of unstructured data, which AI can now combine with traditional quantitative datasets, is the data-related development (supply). Using AI to meet requirements more eﬀiciently is the regulation driver (demand).

⇒ Both halves of C sit in the right bucket.

**Interpretation**

The classification rests on the nature of the driver, not on who pays for it or where it comes from. Every option offers a plausible “because” clause; in the wrong ones the reasoning sounds right and moves the driver across the line.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024), The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence; Schweser-Notes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q41 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap: cloud computing and pre-trained models are business model developments on the supply side. That institutions buy them does not make them demand-side.

b.reason: Sibling swap: competition, the pressure to keep up with rivals fully leveraging AI, is a demand-side driver.

d.reason: Sibling swap: the Transformer and GPU computing are technological developments (supply side). Profitability is a separate demand-side driver.

questions.question: A central bank economist in Australia is writing a retrospective on AI adoption in financial services between the FSB’s 2017 report and its November 2024 update. Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the FSB’s assessment?

options.text: Demand-side forces have been the more influential driver, because profit pressure pushed firms to adopt AI before the technology was ready.
Both sides still matter, but supply-side forces have been the more influential driver, and the launch of ChatGPT was a catalyst for interest.
Supply-side forces drove adoption until the 2017 report, after which competition and regulation replaced them as the main drivers.
The two sides have been equally influential, and the FSB dates the start of AI use in financial services to the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The relative weight**

The 2017 report examined both supply-side and demand-side factors. Both continue to matter, but the evidence indicates that supply-side forces have been the more influential driver.

**Step 2 – The date that matters**

Interest in AI has grown considerably since 2017, and the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was an important catalyst.

⇒ B states both facts in the reading’s own terms.

**Interpretation**

The asymmetry is the tested point: technology, data and business models pushed adoption more than profit, competition and regulation pulled it. ChatGPT raised interest; it did not start AI use in finance, where AI tools have long been used.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q42 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: it reverses the stated dominance; the supply side has been more influential.

c.reason: Scope error on time: 2017 is the date of the report that examined both sides. Since then the supply side has been the more influential driver, not displaced.

d.reason: Two errors: “equally” flattens the stated asymmetry, and AI tools have long been used in financial services; ChatGPT was a catalyst for interest, not the start of use.

questions.question: A quantitative developer at a Hong Kong asset manager is briefing the investment committee on the technological developments behind the firm’s new text-analytics platform. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Embeddings are artificially generated datasets that resemble real-world data, and the Transformer processes text sequentially, one word at a time.
Embeddings are numerical representations of text, images or audio, and the Transformer uses an attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant input.
Embeddings are numerical representations of text, images or audio, and the Transformer’s main contribution was cheaper computing through wider use of GPUs.
GPUs made larger models cheaper to train, but the Transformer’s contribution was limited to structured data, so LLMs rest on earlier architectures.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Embeddings**

Embeddings are numerical representations of data such as text, images or audio, enabled by advances in deep learning. They are what let models process unstructured data.

**Step 2 – The Transformer**

The Transformer revolutionised NLP and laid the foundation for LLMs and GenAI. It uses an attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant parts of the input text, and it processes data in parallel.

⇒ B states both correctly.

**Interpretation**

Of the three technological developments, embeddings and the Transformer are about what models can read; GPUs are about what it costs. Option C blurs that line, which is why it is tempting.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a and Module Quiz 101.1

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q43 and Q44 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.3)

a.reason: Sibling swap and polarity flip: artificially generated look-alike data is synthetic data, a response to the data shortage. The Transformer processes data in parallel, not sequentially.

c.reason: Sibling swap inside the technological developments: cheaper computing through increased computational power and wider GPU use is the third development, separate from the Transformer, which revolutionised natural language processing and laid the foundation for LLMs and GenAI.

d.reason: Polarity flip on the second half: the Transformer revolutionised natural language processing and is the foundation for LLMs. The GPU half is true, which makes the option tempting.

questions.question: A risk manager at a Swedish bank is preparing a training slide that pairs each supply-side driver of AI adoption in the FSB’s framework with the constraint attached to it. Which of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: Technological developments: the shift toward open-source models has made accountability and explainability harder to achieve.
Business model developments: a shortage of skilled staff makes the people needed to build AI models diﬀicult and expensive to hire.
Data-related developments: unstructured data still cannot be combined with traditional quantitative datasets in AI models.
Data-related developments: training needs may exceed the data available, so synthetic data may be needed, raising quality concerns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three pairs**

Technological developments: shortage of human capital that can keep pace. Data-related developments: models need more training data than may exist, so synthetic data may be needed, which raises data quality and model reliability considerations. Business model developments: accountability and explainability challenges.

**Step 2 – Match**

Only D pairs a driver with its own constraint.

⇒ Each supply-side capability arrived with a cost attached to that capability.

**Interpretation**

For a data-hungry bank, the practical message is that synthetic data closes a quantity gap and opens a quality question. Validation has to cover the generated data as well as the model.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap: accountability and explainability are the business model constraint, tied to pre-trained models, not the technological one.

b.reason: Sibling swap: the human capital shortage is the constraint on technological developments.

c.reason: Polarity flip: combining traditional quantitative datasets with unstructured data such as images and videos is the data-related advance, not its constraint.

questions.loText: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demandside drivers.
questions.reading: CI-2: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.topic: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence

questions.question: The CTO of a mid-sized Brazilian bank is deciding whether to license a pre-trained large language model rather than build one in-house. Which of the following assessments is most consistent with the FSB’s account of business model developments?

options.text: Licensing saves time and cost, though accountability and explainability requirements can create challenges; the trend is toward open-source models.
Licensing saves time and cost, and the trend is toward closed-source models, because only closed-source models can be customised to a firm’s needs.
Licensing removes accountability and explainability concerns, because the vendor has already validated the pre-trained model before its release.
Licensing is becoming less common, as falling GPU costs lead most banks to train their own models in-house rather than rely on cloud providers.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why firms license**

The high cost of training models and maintaining the infrastructure has pushed firms toward cloud providers that offer pre-trained AI capabilities. Pre-trained models save time and cost against building in-house.

**Step 2 – The catch**

Accountability and explainability requirements can create challenges for a firm using a model it did not build.

**Step 3 – Which kind**

Pre-trained LLMs come as closed source or open source; the industry trend has shifted toward open source, driven by improving performance relative to closed source. Open-source models are often free, accessible and customisable.

⇒ A has all three.

**Interpretation**

For the CTO, the decision is not build against risk-free buy. Licensing moves cost and time in the bank’s favour, but the bank still has to explain and answer for the model.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q46 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip with a sibling swap: the trend is toward open source, and customisability is an open-source trait.

c.reason: Absolute claim: the reading says accountability and explainability requirements create challenges for pre-trained models; vendor testing does not remove them.

d.reason: Polarity flip: reliance on cloud providers and pre-trained models has increased. Cheaper computing is a technological driver of adoption, not a reason firms are leaving pre-trained models.

questions.question: The COO of a European insurer lists three AI initiatives in a business case: (1) tailored products that reduce customer churn; (2) automated claims handling, with staff moved to sales work that is hard to automate; (3) better forecasts of losses and delinquencies. Under the profitability driver in the FSB’s framework, which of the following mappings is correct?

options.text: (1) cost reduction; (2) revenue growth; (3) improved risk management.
(1) revenue growth; (2) cost reduction; (3) improved risk management.
(1) revenue growth; (2) improved risk management; (3) cost reduction.
(1) improved risk management; (2) cost reduction; (3) revenue growth.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three channels**

Revenue growth: tailored products and services, better onboarding, reduced churn. Cost reduction: automating manual tasks, higher productivity, reallocating resources to revenue-generating work that is hard to automate. Improved risk management: better forecasts of cash flows, losses and delinquencies.

**Step 2 – Map the initiatives**

(1) Lower churn through tailored products is revenue growth. (2) Automation with staff moved to hard-to-automate sales work is cost reduction. (3) Loss and delinquency forecasting is improved risk management.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Two items invite a misfile. Churn sounds like a cost but sits under revenue growth, because it is about keeping customers. Moving staff to sales sounds like revenue but sits under cost reduction, because it is the second half of the automation story.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a and Module Quiz 101.1

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q47 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.6)

a.reason: Role misassignment: reduced churn is revenue growth, and automation with reallocation is cost reduction; the first two are swapped.

c.reason: Role misassignment: forecasting losses and delinquencies is risk management, not cost reduction, and automation is cost reduction.

d.reason: Role misassignment: tailored products that reduce churn are revenue growth, and forecasting is risk management; (1) and (3) are swapped.

questions.loText: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demandside drivers.
questions.reading: CI-2: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.topic: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q48 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (correction box)
questions.question: At a strategy offsite of a Singapore bank, a director argues that because rivals are rolling out GenAI, the bank should shorten its testing programme to keep pace. Which response by the CRO best reflects the FSB’s view of the competition driver?

options.text: Competitive pressure can lower prices and spur innovation, and as a supply-side driver it leaves testing to the vendors that supply the AI tools.
Competitive pressure has been the most influential driver of adoption since 2017, so keeping pace with rivals should take priority over testing.
Competitive pressure can lower prices and spur innovation; the FSB ties its negative outcomes to falling behind rivals rather than to weak testing.
Competitive pressure can bring lower prices and more innovation, but it can also lead to negative outcomes if safeguards and testing fall short.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Place the driver**

Competition is a demand-side driver: pressure to keep up with competitors that are fully leveraging AI, and GenAI in particular.

**Step 2 – Its two outcomes**

As competitive pressure increases, outcomes may be positive (lower prices, greater innovation) or negative if safeguards and testing are insuﬀicient.

⇒ Cutting testing to keep pace is the route to the negative outcome.

**Interpretation**

The director’s argument fails on the reading’s own terms: competition is a reason to adopt, not a reason to test less. The same pressure reappears in CI-2 c, where competitive pressure and easy access to GenAI may speed deployment and introduce new risks.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a and 101.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q48 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (correction box) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: competition is a demand-side driver, and the reading ties its outcome to safeguards and testing, not to who supplies the tools.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the weight: the evidence indicates that supply-side forces have been the more influential driver.

c.reason: Scope error: the negative outcomes the reading links to competition arise when safeguards and testing are insuﬀicient, not from falling behind rivals. Dropping that downside is the misreading the class notes’ Figure CI-2.1 caption invites (see the correction box).

questions.topic: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q49 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a
questions.question: The head of compliance at a Dubai-based bank is explaining to the audit committee why regulation appears among the drivers of AI adoption in the FSB’s framework. Which of the following explanations is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Regulators now require institutions to deploy AI in their compliance functions, so regulation acts as a mandate rather than as a motive.
Expanding rules raise the cost of experimenting with AI, so regulation acts mainly as a brake that offsets the supply-side drivers.
Firms use AI to meet requirements more eﬀiciently as rules on data protection, guidance on AI and international standards expand.
Regulation is a supply-side driver, because it determines which AI models vendors are allowed to sell to regulated institutions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the driver is**

Companies need to enhance compliance and meet regulatory requirements more eﬀiciently, and AI is increasingly viewed as a tool that strengthens compliance capabilities.

**Step 2 – Why it is growing**

Rules on data protection, guidance on AI development and adoption, and international standards continue to expand.

⇒ More rules raise the value of eﬀicient compliance, so they pull AI in: a demand-side motive.

**Interpretation**

Regulation here works like profitability: it gives firms a reason to want AI. The same idea seen from the firm’s side is RegTech, an industry use case in CI-2 b.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q49 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a; CI notes CI-2 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.8)

a.reason: Scope error: the driver is the firm’s need to comply eﬀiciently; the reading describes no mandate to adopt AI.

b.reason: Polarity flip: expanding rules increase the demand for AI as a compliance tool; the reading lists regulation as a driver of adoption, not a brake.

d.reason: Sibling swap: regulation is one of the three demand-side factors.

questions.question: A model risk oﬀicer at a Swiss private bank is drafting a training note on how the GenAI assistant the bank has just licensed differs from its long-standing ML credit models, drawing on the FSB’s account of developments since 2017. Which of the following statements should she include?

options.text: GenAI builds on the Transformer architecture, the foundation for LLMs, and its outputs are mostly unstructured text, so error rates are harder to establish.
GenAI differs mainly in using only structured quantitative data, which is why it needs less training data than earlier ML models and no synthetic data at all.
GenAI’s characteristic inaccuracy is data poisoning, in which the model produces a highly confident but incorrect answer without outside interference.
The FSB places LLMs with decision trees and clustering among established predictive tools, so the GenAI assistant needs no new validation approach.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What GenAI is built on**

The Transformer architecture revolutionised natural language processing and laid the foundation for LLMs and GenAI; embeddings from deep learning let models process unstructured data.

**Step 2 – What changes for validation**

LLM outputs are typically generated as unstructured text, so assessing their accuracy is hard and outcome analysis and error rates are often diﬀicult to establish. The GenAI-specific inaccuracy is the hallucination, a highly confident but incorrect response.

⇒ A gives the foundation and the validation consequence correctly.

**Interpretation**

This is shape A14·S1 seen from the FSB’s side: the assistant’s text output needs different checks from a credit model’s numerical forecasts. The IMF’s version, its two model groups, is Workbook A14.1 under CI-1 a.

**LO:** CI-2 a: Explain key developments in AI since 2017, differentiating between supply-side drivers and demand-side drivers. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.a and 101.c

CI-2 • The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (FSB, November 2024) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.a and 101.c; CI notes CI-2 a, c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 a.9)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the advance is processing unstructured data, and modern models often need more training data than is available, hence synthetic data.

c.reason: Sibling swap on the failure mode: a highly confident but incorrect response is a hallucination. Data poisoning is a cyber attack that deliberately manipulates training data or model weights (CI-2 c).

d.reason: Role misassignment and sibling swap: grouping models into established AI/ML (decision trees, clustering, NLP) and sophisticated AI (including LLMs) is the IMF’s scheme in CI-1 a, not the FSB’s, and it places LLMs in the sophisticated group.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Korean bank is mapping four AI projects to the FSB’s industry use-case areas: (1) ML models that add behavioural data to credit scores in loan preapproval; (2) GenAI tools that modernise legacy code; (3) LLMs that read news text to gauge market sentiment for trading signals; (4) AI screening of clients for trade-based money laundering. Which of the following mappings is correct?

options.text: (1) customers; (2) operations; (3) trading and portfolio management; (4) regulatory compliance.
(1) customers; (2) operations; (3) operations; (4) regulatory compliance.
(1) regulatory compliance; (2) operations; (3) trading and portfolio management; (4) customers.
(1) customers; (2) trading and portfolio management; (3) customers; (4) regulatory compliance.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The four industry areas**

Customers, operations, trading and portfolio management, and regulatory compliance.

**Step 2 – Place each project**

(1) ML that supplements credit scoring in preapproval is customer-focused. (2) Legacy code modernisation is a GenAI operations use. (3) Sentiment in text for trading is trading and portfolio management. (4) Detecting trade-based money laundering is regulatory compliance (RegTech).

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Classify by the function the tool serves for the firm. Text processing appears in several areas (chatbots, sentiment, inspection reports), so the input type does not decide the area; the purpose does.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024), The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.1)

b.reason: Sibling swap: sentiment analysis of text for trading signals is a trading and portfolio management use, not an operations (back-oﬀice) one.

c.reason: Sibling swap: credit preapproval is customer-focused, and money-laundering screening is regulatory compliance; (1) and (4) are swapped.

d.reason: Sibling swap: legacy code modernisation is operations, and sentiment analysis serves trading, not customers.

questions.question: The head of retail lending at a Mexican bank is describing to the board how AI is used in the bank’s customer-focused activities. Which of the following statements is most consistent with the FSB’s description of such use cases?

options.text: ML models have replaced traditional credit scoring in loan preapproval, and GenAI has moved chatbots from rules-based systems to LLM-based ones.
ML models supplement traditional credit scoring with additional data and behavioural insights, and GenAI has moved chatbots to LLM-based systems.
ML models supplement traditional credit scoring with additional data, and GenAI has moved chatbots from LLM-based systems back to rules-based ones.
ML models supplement traditional credit scoring with additional data, but customer uses stop at lending, with no role in pricing insurance policies.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit**

In loan preapproval, banks increasingly rely on ML models to supplement traditional credit scoring with additional data and behavioural insights.

**Step 2 – Chatbots**

GenAI has enabled more sophisticated chatbot interactions by shifting from rules-based systems to LLM-based approaches.

⇒ B states both correctly.

**Interpretation**

The two verbs carry the question: ML supplements the traditional score, and the chatbot move runs toward LLMs. Customer-focused uses also include targeted marketing, adviser matching and insurance pricing.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q52 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.2)

a.reason: Absolute claim: ML supplements traditional credit scoring; the reading does not say it has replaced it.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the shift ran from rules-based systems to LLM-based ones.

d.reason: Scope error: the customer area also covers insurance, where AI improves the pricing and risk management of policies by predicting policy risk and insured behaviour.

questions.question: The head of model validation at a UK bank is ranking the bank’s operations-focused AI applications to decide which to validate first. Which of the following applications does the FSB describe as more complex and potentially riskier than the others?

options.text: Voice transcription of recorded client calls for the bank’s complaints-handling team.
Information search and retrieval across the bank’s internal policy and procedure documents.
Modernisation of legacy code in the bank’s payments and regulatory reporting systems.
Optimisation of regulatory capital requirements, such as estimating default probabilities.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The operations list**

Operations (back-oﬀice) uses include model risk management, capital optimisation, code generation, market impact analysis, and volatility and liquidity risk management, plus the GenAI uses: content generation, search and retrieval, code generation, legacy code modernisation and voice transcription.

**Step 2 – The one the reading flags**

More complex and potentially riskier applications involve optimising regulatory capital requirements, such as estimating default probabilities.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

For the validation queue, the reading’s flag fits the stakes: capital optimisation feeds regulatory capital requirements and default estimates, while transcription, retrieval and legacy code work are back-oﬀice eﬀiciency uses.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q54 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.3)

a.reason: Sibling swap on the risk tier: voice transcription is one of the routine GenAI operations uses.

b.reason: Sibling swap on the risk tier: search and retrieval is a routine GenAI operations use.

c.reason: Sibling swap on the risk tier: legacy code modernisation is listed among GenAI’s operations uses, not singled out as more complex and potentially riskier.

questions.question: A mid-sized Polish insurer has a small IT team and few staff with specialised coding skills. Its COO asks how GenAI could change the operations-focused AI the firm is able to use. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: GenAI can broaden access to advanced tools, such as code generation and legacy code modernisation, for firms that lacked enough specialised coders.
GenAI mainly benefits firms that already employ large teams of specialised coders, so the insurer should expect to fall further behind its rivals.
GenAI’s operations uses are limited to content generation and voice transcription; code generation still needs specialised in-house coding staff.
GenAI code generation is a trading and portfolio management use, so it would help the insurer’s investment desk rather than its back-oﬀice functions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What GenAI added to operations**

Content generation, information search and retrieval, code generation, legacy code modernisation and voice transcription.

**Step 2 – Who gains**

An additional benefit of GenAI is that it broadens access to advanced tools for firms that previously lacked suﬀicient staff with specialised coding skills.

⇒ The insurer is exactly the firm the reading describes.

**Interpretation**

GenAI lowers the skill barrier inside the firm. The same accessibility cuts the other way in CI-2 c: easier access to GenAI also lowers barriers for less sophisticated threat actors.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q60 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.4)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the stated benefit goes to firms without enough specialised coders.

c.reason: Scope error: code generation and legacy code modernisation are among GenAI’s operations uses, and the point is that they need fewer specialised coders.

d.reason: Sibling swap: code generation is an operations (back-oﬀice) use case.

questions.question: The head of systematic trading at a Swiss asset manager is presenting to the risk committee on how GenAI supports the firm’s trading and portfolio management. Which of the following statements is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: GenAI supports reinforcement learning for trade execution and sentiment analysis of text, but LLMs capture only the obvious relationships between words.
GenAI supports reinforcement learning for trade execution and sentiment analysis of text, with LLMs capturing obvious and subtle word relationships.
GenAI supports trade execution, but sentiment analysis of text is a customer-focused use, because it draws on customer communications and complaints.
GenAI supports trade execution and sentiment analysis, but the FSB sees no role for it in streamlining portfolio analysis and decision-making.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Execution and sentiment**

GenAI has been valuable for firms implementing reinforcement learning for trade execution and for assessing market sentiment embedded in text data.

**Step 2 – What LLMs add**

LLMs can identify both obvious and subtle relationships between words that may be diﬀicult to capture with traditional approaches.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The subtle relationships are the point: they are what traditional text methods miss. GenAI also supports portfolio management with automation tools that streamline analysis and decision-making.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q55 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: LLMs capture both obvious and subtle relationships; the subtle ones are their advantage over traditional approaches.

c.reason: Sibling swap: sentiment analysis of text for trading sits in trading and portfolio management. Customer-focused uses are credit, marketing, advisers, insurance and chatbots.

d.reason: Scope error: GenAI also supports portfolio management through automation tools that streamline analysis and decision-making.

questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q53 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b (Figure 101.2, Module Quiz 101.2)
questions.question: The head of data science at a digital bank is tagging three systems by the task each performs, following the task categories in the reading: (1) a check that matches a new customer’s live selfie to the passport photo; (2) a model that projects next quarter’s delinquencies from past repayment data; (3) a tool that builds an individual profile of each client to tailor offers. Which tagging is correct?

options.text: (1) recognition; (2) goal-driven optimisation; (3) personalisation.
(1) personalisation; (2) forecasting; (3) recognition.
(1) recognition; (2) forecasting; (3) personalisation.
(1) recognition; (2) forecasting; (3) goal-driven optimisation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name each task**

(1) Matching a selfie to a passport photo classifies an image: the recognition task, of which facial recognition is the reading’s example. (2) Projecting delinquencies from past repayment data predicts a future outcome from history: forecasting. (3) Building an individual profile of each client is personalisation.

**Step 2 – The learning types that go with them**

Recognition uses supervised classification of images, voice and text; forecasting uses supervised learning on historical data to predict future outcomes; personalisation develops individual profiles using supervised or reinforcement learning.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The grid works in one direction: identify what the system does (recognise, forecast, optimise, personalise) and the learning type follows. The same delinquency model would count as improved risk management under the profitability driver in CI-2 a; the two frameworks classify different things. Onboarding verification is also where GenAI deepfakes and fake IDs attack (CI-2 c, fraud).

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b and Module Quiz 101.2

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q53 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b (Figure 101.2, Module Quiz 101.2) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.6)

a.reason: Sibling swap on (2): predicting from historical data is forecasting; goal-driven optimisation determines optimal solutions to decision problems.

b.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (3): matching a selfie to a photo is recognition (supervised classification of images), and building individual profiles is personalisation.

d.reason: Sibling swap on (3): developing individual profiles is personalisation, not goal-driven optimisation.

questions.question: A consultant is advising both a commercial bank and its national central bank on AI. The bank uses AI to investigate sanctions evasion by its clients; the central bank uses AI to oversee the payment system. Under the FSB’s classification of use cases, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Both are SupTech, because each uses AI to apply financial regulation, whoever runs the tool.
Both are RegTech, because each uses AI to detect breaches of rules in the financial system.
The bank’s use is SupTech, because it serves supervisors, and the central bank’s is RegTech.
The bank’s use is RegTech, an industry use case, and the central bank’s use is SupTech.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – RegTech**

Using AI to meet regulatory requirements, including AML, CFT and investigating sanctions evasion, is regulatory technology: an industry use case in the regulatory compliance area.

**Step 2 – SupTech**

Technology used by supervisory authorities is SupTech. Central banks use AI for information collection, statistical compilation and payment system oversight.

⇒ Same broad purpose, different actor: the bank’s use is RegTech and the central bank’s is SupTech.

**Interpretation**

The test is who runs the tool, not what it does. The class notes’ Figure CI-2.2 makes the same point: the same AML technology is RegTech in a bank and SupTech in a central bank, so the consultant should file the two projects on opposite sides of the line.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Figure CI-2.2) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.7)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the bank is a regulated firm meeting its own requirements, so its tool is RegTech.

b.reason: Role misassignment: payment system oversight by a central bank is SupTech.

c.reason: Role misassignment both ways: serving supervisors does not make a firm’s tool SupTech, and the central bank’s tool is SupTech.

questions.question: A supervision director at an Asian central bank is drafting a three-year SupTech roadmap and wants to separate the current uses of AI by authorities from those the FSB presents as potential future applications. Which of the following is a potential future application?

options.text: Reviewing large volumes of examination documents to draft inspection reports and summaries.
Using LLMs to generate customised error messages that support supervisory workflows.
Using GenAI to model stress tests and bank runs by simulating social media interactions.
Using alternative data and real-time economic analysis in supervisory assessments.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Current SupTech**

Information collection, statistical compilation and payment system oversight; alternative data; real-time economic analysis; LLM experiments for analysis and research; reviewing examination documents to draft inspection reports; LLM-generated customised error messages.

**Step 2 – Potential future**

Using GenAI to model stress tests and bank runs by simulating social media interactions.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The roadmap should put simulation in its later years. The FSB adds that SupTech will need more AI capability so that authorities can keep pace with AI adoption in the institutions they supervise.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q58 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.8)

a.reason: Tense error: drafting inspection reports from large volumes of examination documents is a current GenAI and NLP use.

b.reason: Tense error: LLMs already generate customised error messages to support supervisory workflows.

d.reason: Tense error: alternative data and real-time economic analysis are current uses.

questions.question: The head of strategy at a South African bank is preparing a five-year view of how GenAI will be used across the financial industry. Which of the following statements is most consistent with the FSB’s assessment?

options.text: Adoption has been cautious so far, but accessibility and strong interest may bring faster deployment and deeper use in critical operations.
GenAI may already be embedded in core banking at most institutions, so the FSB expects its deployment to slow from here as use matures.
GenAI will stay confined to back-oﬀice drafting, since the FSB sees no role for it in investment advice or tailored product recommendations.
Adoption has been rapid and broad, because legitimate institutions have adopted new AI tools faster than malicious actors have been able to.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where adoption stands**

Financial institutions’ adoption of GenAI has been cautious so far.

**Step 2 – Where it may go**

The accessibility of the technology and strong industry interest may lead to more rapid deployment and deeper integration into critical operations: investment advisory services, price discovery, coding assistance for claims processing, loan servicing, core banking and payment execution, risk management and compliance, and tailored product recommendations.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The emerging use cases are where CI-2 c bites: deeper use in critical operations raises the stakes of shared models, shared vendors and model error.

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b and 101.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b and 101.c; CI notes CI-2 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.9)

b.reason: Polarity flip: adoption has been cautious so far, and faster deployment is the expectation.

c.reason: Scope error: investment advisory services and tailored product recommendations are among the named potential applications.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the reading contrasts cautious, risk-averse legitimate actors with malicious actors who are often willing to adopt AI rapidly (CI-2 c).

questions.question: An economist at a national financial stability authority is designing a survey of AI adoption by banks, insurers and asset managers. Which of the following cautions about measuring adoption is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: Comprehensive adoption data already exist in supervisory returns, so the survey’s main use is to forecast GenAI’s move into critical operations.
Comprehensive adoption data are lacking, and competitive pressures may open a gap between perceived and actual AI use.
Adoption data are most complete for institutions outside traditional regulatory frameworks, whose AI use is the most visible to authorities.
Adoption data are lacking only for GenAI; established AI used in liquidity, market and credit risk management is well documented.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The data gap**

A key challenge in assessing adoption is the lack of comprehensive data on how far it has gone.

**Step 2 – The distortion**

Competitive pressures may also contribute to a gap between perceived and actual AI use.

⇒ The survey should not take reported or perceived use at face value.

**Interpretation**

The reading names the gap and its source (competitive pressure) without stating its direction, so the safe reading is that perception and reality can differ. Closing data gaps is also the first of the FSB’s priorities for authorities (CI-2 c).

**LO:** CI-2 b: Identify and analyze existing and emerging AI use cases in financial services, including industry use cases as well as regulatory and supervisory use cases. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.b and 101.c

CI-2 • The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (FSB, November 2024) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q59 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.b and 101.c; CI notes CI-2 b, c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 b.10)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the stated problem is that comprehensive data on adoption are lacking.

c.reason: Polarity flip: AI use is even less visible to authorities at institutions outside traditional regulatory frameworks.

d.reason: Scope error: the reading says representative data on AI use in risk management functions such as liquidity, market and credit risk are lacking too.

options.text: AI use has spread across core operations and business lines, while models rely more on training data that may be unavailable, opaque or unstructured.
AI use has spread across core operations, but its training data have become more transparent and structured, making model behaviour easier to verify.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The four developments**

Expanded AI integration across core operations and business lines; greater reliance on training data that may be unavailable, opaque or highly unstructured; dependence on cloud providers and a concentrated market for advanced chips; and GenAI and LLM breakthroughs, where competitive pressure and easy access may speed deployment.

**Step 2 – Match**

A states the first two correctly.

⇒ The report should open with wider integration and less transparent data.

**Interpretation**

The FSB says these developments interact with the vulnerabilities: opaque training data reappears under model risk and data quality, and dependence on cloud providers and chips under third-party concentration. Authorities face two further challenges: limited data on AI use and the uncertainty created by rapid innovation.

questions.question: An economist at a national competition authority is assessing two developments in the market for LLM and GenAI service providers: (1) growing client demand for models that can perform a wide range of GenAI tasks; (2) advances in model architecture that improve scalability and eﬀiciency. Under the FSB’s assessment, how is each development most likely to affect provider concentration?

options.text: (1) supports competition; (2) supports competition.
(1) raises concentration; (2) raises concentration.
(1) raises concentration; (2) supports competition.
(1) supports competition; (2) raises concentration.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Forces that raise concentration**

Complexity and costs; vertical integration; supply chain bottlenecks (scarce GPUs); investment behaviour (incumbents funding new AI labs); multimodality (demand for broad models favours providers with broad capabilities).

**Step 2 – Forces that may support competition**

Hardware competition; open-source models; architectural innovations that improve scalability and eﬀiciency and could lower barriers to entry; domain- and task-specific models.

**Step 3 – Place the two developments**

(1) Demand for models that perform a wide range of GenAI tasks is multimodality: it may favour providers with broad capabilities, so it raises concentration. (2) Advances in architecture that improve scalability and eﬀiciency are architectural innovations: they could lower barriers to entry, so they support competition.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The rule of thumb: anything that rewards breadth and scale favours incumbents; anything that lowers the cost of entry favours challengers. Multimodality and architectural innovations are the two items the class notes’ table leaves out (see the correction box), which is why this question tests exactly that pair.

**LO:** CI-2 c: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration; Market correlations; Cyber risks; Model risk, data, and governance; Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.c and Module Quiz 101.3

a.reason: Sibling swap on (1): multimodality raises concentration, because demand for models that do a wide range of tasks favours providers with broad capabilities.

b.reason: Sibling swap on (2): architectural innovations that improve scalability and eﬀiciency could lower barriers to entry, which supports competition.

d.reason: Sibling swap on both: the two developments sit on the opposite sides of the FSB’s ledger.

questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian bank that relies on a single cloud service provider for its GenAI models and computing capacity is reviewing the bank’s third-party risk policy. Which of the following assessments is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: It exposes the bank to supply chain disruptions and cyber events at key vendors, and calls for periodic assessments, vendor inventories and monitoring.
The provider’s own certifications of its controls can stand in for the bank’s periodic assessments, since the provider is better placed to judge its own risks.
A thorough assessment at onboarding meets the third-party standards, so ongoing monitoring is needed only if the provider later changes its service terms.
Provider concentration brings only costs for the bank, since the FSB sees no offsetting benefit for risk management from coordination or technological synergies.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the dependence exposes**

Service provider concentration and third-party dependencies expose institutions to operational risks, including supply chain disruptions and cyber events affecting key vendors.

**Step 2 – What the bank is expected to do**

Institutions are expected to apply third-party risk management standards: periodic risk assessments, detailed vendor inventories, and ongoing monitoring and due diligence.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The standards are the institution’s to apply; the provider’s size does not move the obligation. The FSB also notes an offset: more coordination and technological synergies may make risk management more effective and eﬀicient.

**LO:** CI-2 c: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration; Market correlations; Cyber risks; Model risk, data, and governance; Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.c

b.reason: Role misassignment: the standards place periodic assessment and due diligence on the institution; nothing in the reading lets the provider’s own certification replace them.

c.reason: Scope error: the standards call for periodic assessments and ongoing monitoring, not a single check at onboarding.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the FSB says increased coordination and technological synergies may enhance the effectiveness and eﬀiciency of risk management.

questions.question: A securities regulator observes that GenAI-generated research text is increasingly entering the datasets used to train new models, and that AI-driven systems at several firms now act on market signals far faster than before. Which of the following assessments is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: Re-using GenAI output as training data diversifies what new models learn from, and faster automated decisions spread firms’ reactions over time.
Faster automated decisions can synchronise behaviour, but re-using GenAI output in training data has no bearing on the correlation between models.
Re-using GenAI output in training data can raise correlation, and faster automated decisions can synchronise reactions to market conditions.
Correlation arises only when firms use identical in-house models, so neither the reuse of training data nor decision speed changes it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The feedback**

Correlations may increase if GenAI-generated outputs are incorporated into future training datasets.

**Step 2 – The speed channel**

Greater automation and faster decision-making in financial markets can lead to more synchronised behaviour, such as coordinated reactions to market conditions or shifts in corporate deposit activity, which may amplify market stress.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Both observations point the same way: correlation can build through what models learn from and through how fast they act on it. The third channel, pre-trained core models that share architectures and training data, is the subject of Workbook A14.3 under CI-1 c.

b.reason: Scope error: it drops the feedback channel; correlations may also increase if GenAI-generated outputs are incorporated into future training datasets.

d.reason: Absolute claim: correlation arises from similar models and data sources, including shared pre-trained models, and from synchronised automated behaviour; it is not limited to identical in-house models.

questions.question: A securities regulator is reviewing its policy toolkit after several episodes in which AI-driven trading strategies at different firms reacted to the same signals at the same time. Which of the following approaches best reflects the mitigants the FSB identifies for AI-driven market correlation?

options.text: Rely mainly on third-party risk standards, such as vendor inventories and periodic assessments, which the FSB names as the main correlation mitigant.
Use volatility control mechanisms such as circuit breakers and enhanced transparency requirements, complemented by consistent monitoring and surveillance.
Require firms to build their models around a single common risk management standard, so that supervisors can compare model outputs across firms.
Discourage customised AI trading strategies, since the FSB identifies customised strategies as the main source of correlated selling in stressed markets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The named mitigants**

Volatility control mechanisms such as circuit breakers, and enhanced transparency requirements.

**Step 2 – The complements**

Consistent monitoring and improved surveillance and data mechanisms.

⇒ B lists the FSB’s toolkit.

**Interpretation**

One way to read the list (Figure 2): transparency at opaque model design, circuit breakers at the volatility itself, monitoring across the loop. The FSB presents them as reducing the impact; none removes the vulnerability. AI can also reduce correlation through more customised strategies, which is a reason not to discourage them.

questions.question: The CISO of a central securities depository, a financial market infrastructure (FMI), is briefing the board on how AI changes the institution’s cyber exposure. Which of the following statements is most consistent with the FSB?

options.text: Attack vectors have grown as AI systems take input through many channels and use larger datasets, and an FMI attack can amplify volatility and liquidity strains.
Attack vectors have narrowed as AI is concentrated in a few well-defended providers, so FMIs face less AI-related cyber risk than smaller financial firms do.
LLMs strengthen cyber defences but cannot themselves be exploited to carry out attacks, so the main threat to the FMI remains conventional malicious code.
Cyber events matter for financial stability mainly through direct operational losses, and a loss of confidence plays little part in how their effects spread across markets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the attack surface grows**

Modern AI systems allow interaction through many channels and rely on increasingly large datasets, so the number of potential attack vectors, the pathways an attacker can use to compromise a system, has grown significantly.

**Step 2 – Why an FMI matters**

The sector is particularly vulnerable when attacks target central banks, critical service providers, FMIs, essential services that cannot easily be substituted, or other highly important firms. Service disruptions and declines in confidence can amplify volatility, liquidity vulnerabilities and operational losses.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

For the depository’s board the message is two-sided: AI widens the ways in, and the institution’s systemic role widens the damage. The FSB’s best practices apply: an AI risk management framework (new, or AI added to the existing one) and AI questions in vendor due diligence.

**LO:** CI-2 c: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration; Market correlations; Cyber risks; Model risk, data, and governance; Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.c; CI notes CI-2 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 c.6)

c.reason: Absolute claim: LLMs themselves could be exploited to carry out certain types of attack.

d.reason: Scope error: declines in confidence, together with service disruptions, are what amplify volatility, liquidity vulnerabilities and operational losses.

questions.question: At a cyber risk workshop for regulators in Asia, a speaker summarises how GenAI shifts the balance between attackers and defenders in the financial sector. Which of the following statements best reflects the FSB’s assessment?

options.text: Attackers and legitimate users may gain about equally, because GenAI’s defensive uses, such as faster detection, offset its many new attack vectors.
Attackers may gain more in the short term, mainly because GenAI raises the barriers to entry and so favours highly sophisticated, well-funded attackers.
Attackers may gain more than legitimate users in the short term, partly as cautious firms adopt slowly while attackers adopt fast and take risks.
Attackers may gain more over the long term, because defensive benefits such as faster incident response take years to reach firms’ systems.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Both sides gain**

Legitimate users benefit through automation of routine tasks, faster incident response, better detection of cyber events, more effective diagnosis of malicious code, and better employee training.

**Step 2 – But not equally, and not forever**

Bad actors may benefit even more in the short term, and malicious actors may be able to exploit AI tools more rapidly. Part of the reason is behavioural: cautious, risk-averse legitimate actors create an asymmetry with malicious actors who are often willing to adopt AI rapidly and take greater risks. Over the long term, legitimate users are expected to gain more (SchweserNotes Module Quiz 101.3 answer key).

⇒ C, with both qualifiers: “more” and “in the short term”.

**Interpretation**

This is shape A14·S2’s “short-term edge of bad actors”. Every option is hedged, so the wording gives nothing away: what separates them is the direction of the edge, its horizon and its cause.

**LO:** CI-2 c: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration; Market correlations; Cyber risks; Model risk, data, and governance; Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.c and Module Quiz 101.3

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 101.c; CI notes CI-2 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-2 c.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip on the asymmetry: legitimate users do benefit, but bad actors may benefit even more in the short term, so the gains are not equal.

b.reason: Polarity flip: GenAI lowers barriers to entry for less sophisticated threat actors.

d.reason: Polarity flip on the horizon: the bad actors’ edge is a short-term one; the Module Quiz 101.3 answer key adds that legitimate users are expected to gain more over the long term.
