questions.question: The head of digital assets at a Toronto pension fund lists three concerns about a proposed ledger: (1) the fund’s usual counterparties are not on the ledger, so ownership cannot pass to them on it; (2) the operator could move the fund’s tokens without the fund’s consent; (3) coupon payments would still have to be calculated and sent by hand. Which features of a tokenized ledger do the three concerns relate to?

options.text: (1) trust; (2) sharedness; (3) programmability.
(1) sharedness; (2) programmability; (3) trust.
(1) sharedness; (2) trust; (3) programmability.
(1) programmability; (2) trust; (3) sharedness.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Concern (1)**

Sharedness: the ledger is accessible to all relevant parties and ownership can be transferred between them. Counterparties who are not on the ledger cannot receive ownership on it.

**Step 2 – Concern (2)**

Trust: users can be confident that their assets cannot be moved without their consent.

**Step 3 – Concern (3)**

Programmability: smart contracts automate instructions such as paying interest.

⇒ Access and transfer, consent, automation: sharedness, trust, programmability.

**Interpretation**

Each feature answers a different question (Figure 2): who can reach the record, can it be altered, can the ledger act by itself. Matching a concern to its question is the quickest way through a feature-mapping item.

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (2): access for counterparties is sharedness, and protection against moves without consent is trust.

b.reason: Sibling swap on (2) and (3): consent is trust, and automated coupons are programmability.

d.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (3): reaching counterparties is sharedness, and automating coupons is programmability.

questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies

questions.question: A structurer at a Hong Kong bank proposes a tokenized note whose smart contract the ledger operator would rewrite by hand whenever the parties want to change its terms. A colleague objects that the proposal misreads how the IMF note describes smart contracts. Which description supports the colleague?

options.text: Smart contracts are instructions that users send to a separate database operator, who executes them once the parties have agreed the terms.
Smart contracts are immutable code that automates instructions, so the note’s transfers and payments operate exactly as intended.
Smart contracts are digitised legal agreements attached to the token record, which give holders a claim but execute nothing by themselves.
Smart contracts are the ledger’s trust feature, which ensures that the operator cannot move a holder’s assets without the holder’s consent.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The reading’s definition**

Programmability lets the ledger incorporate smart contracts: immutable code that automates instructions. They can create assets, transfer assets only when conditions are met and ensure compliance with rules.

**Step 2 – What smart contracts make possible**

This capability makes it possible to bundle complex transactions together and ensure they operate exactly as intended.

⇒ A contract the operator rewrites on request is not what the reading calls a smart contract.

**Interpretation**

The reading’s own examples (coupon-paying transferable bonds, transfers restricted to qualified investors) work because the rules are written in advance and execute automatically.

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a and 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q104 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.5)

a.reason: Sibling swap: users sending instructions to a separate database operator is the traditional set-up that the ledger’s internal programmability replaces (CI-7 e).

c.reason: Form without function: a document attached to a record automates nothing, whereas a smart contract executes instructions.

d.reason: Feature swap: protection against moves without consent is trust. Smart contracts belong to programmability.

questions.source: New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a
questions.question: A consultant reviewing a ledger for a Mumbai exchange finds that all relevant parties can access it, ownership records update directly on it, and smart contracts automate payments. However, the ledger’s rules let the operator reassign holdings without the owner’s consent. Which conclusion is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: It can support tokenization effectively, because the features vary by degree and two strong features can make up for a weak third.
It can support tokenization effectively, because trust comes from contract law rather than from the ledger, so only two features matter.
It cannot support tokenization effectively, because it lacks sharedness: holdings that an operator can reassign are not truly shared.
It cannot support tokenization effectively, because it lacks trust: assets must not be movable without the owner’s consent.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Check the features present**

Access for all relevant parties and direct record updates: sharedness. Smart contracts automating payments: programmability.

**Step 2 – Check the feature missing**

Trust requires that assets cannot be moved without the owner’s consent. An operator who can reassign holdings breaks exactly that.

**Step 3 – Apply the rule**

Tokenization functions effectively only when the ledger provides all three features.

⇒ Two out of three is not enough.

**Interpretation**

“The features vary by degree” means a ledger can offer more or less of each; it does not mean one can be absent. The class notes: a ledger missing any one of the three cannot support tokenization.

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.6)

a.reason: Misreads “vary by degree” as permission to trade one feature off against another; all three are essential.

b.reason: Scope error: trust is one of the three features of the ledger itself, covering accurate records and consent, so it cannot be dropped from the ledger.

c.reason: Feature swap: the defect is the operator’s power to move assets without consent, which is trust. Access and direct record updates (sharedness) are present.

questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a and 106.e; CI notes CI-7 a (correction box)
questions.question: A fintech supervisor at a central bank is reviewing a firm’s claim that its centrally operated platform “cannot host tokens, because tokens can exist only on a distributed ledger”. Which response is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The claim is right for native tokens only: non-native tokens can sit on a central platform, because their assets exist off the ledger.
The claim is right: trust in a tokenized system can come only from consensus among many validators, which a single operator cannot supply.
The claim is wrong: tokens sit on a digital ledger, and trust can come from one operator’s credibility and oversight, not only from DLT.
The claim is wrong, but only because a central platform is a common ledger model, which holds the original assets in escrow for users.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where tokens live**

Tokens are assets or representations of assets created on a digital ledger. Nothing in the definition requires the ledger to be distributed.

**Step 2 – Where trust can come from**

Trust in digital ledgers can be established through single-operator systems, permissionless DLT or permissioned DLT. In a single-operator system one entity manages records and executes and confirms transactions, and trust rests on its credibility, supervision and oversight.

⇒ A centrally run platform can host tokens if it supplies trust, sharedness and programmability.

**Interpretation**

The class notes’ phrase “a set of tools built on distributed ledgers” is narrower than the reading (see the correction box). The design question is how well each trust model works and how it fails (CI-7 e), not whether a central ledger is allowed at all.

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a and 106.e

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a and 106.e; CI notes CI-7 a (correction box) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.7)

a.reason: Invented split: the native and non-native distinction is about where the asset lives, not about which kind of ledger may host the token.

b.reason: Absolute claim: consensus is how permissionless and permissioned DLT build trust; a single-operator system builds it through the operator’s credibility and oversight.

d.reason: Axis confusion: the common ledger model (escrow and certificates) is a way of achieving sharedness. It does not describe a centrally operated platform as such.

questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q108 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a
questions.question: A board member at a Seoul brokerage argues that a ledger restricted to approved participants can never provide sharedness, because sharedness means that anyone in the world can read and use the ledger. Which response best reflects the reading’s definition?

options.text: The board member is wrong: sharedness requires access for all relevant parties, transfers between them and records updated on the ledger.
The board member is right: sharedness means no party can move assets without the owner’s consent, which a restricted ledger cannot ensure.
The board member is right: sharedness requires a ledger open to anyone, so a restricted ledger can be trusted and programmable but not shared.
The board member is wrong: sharedness means that the code and the database are integrated, which any ledger running smart contracts provides.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The definition**

Sharedness: the ledger is accessible to all relevant parties, asset ownership can be transferred between them, and ownership records are updated directly on the ledger.

**Step 2 – Apply it**

A ledger limited to approved participants provides sharedness if the relevant parties are on it and can transfer ownership on it. Who may join or validate is a separate design choice about trust (CI-7 e).

⇒ “All relevant parties” is not “anyone in the world”.

**Interpretation**

The board member has merged two questions: who can reach the record (sharedness) and who is allowed to join and validate (the trust model, for example permissioned DLT).

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a and 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q108 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.8)

b.reason: Feature swap: consent protection is the definition of trust, not of sharedness.

c.reason: Scope error: the definition asks for access by all relevant parties, not openness to anyone.

d.reason: Feature swap: integration of code and database is how the reading describes programmability (CI-7 e).

questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q106 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a
questions.question: The head of capital markets at a development bank wants a new bond that (1) exists only on a ledger, (2) can be transferred only with the holder’s authorisation, and (3) pays coupons and restricts transfers to qualified investors automatically. Which design best meets all three requirements?

options.text: A non-native token on a shared ledger, backed by a conventional bond held with a custodian, which pays the coupons to holders.
A native token on a ledger whose smart contracts pay coupons and screen buyers, and whose holdings cannot move without consent.
A native token on a shared ledger, with the qualified-investor limit enforced through the ledger’s trust feature rather than code.
A bond migrated from a conventional register but kept live there, and mirrored on the ledger so that both records can be updated.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Requirement (1) fixes the token type**

“Exists only on a ledger” is the definition of a native token. A non-native token represents an asset that exists outside the ledger.

**Step 2 – Requirements (2) and (3) fix the features**

Transfer only with the holder’s authorisation is trust. Automatic coupons and a qualified-investor restriction are programmability: the reading’s own smart-contract examples. The ledger must also be shared so that ownership can pass between holders.

⇒ A native token on a trusted, shared and programmable ledger, with smart contracts doing the paying and the screening.

**Interpretation**

Read requirement lists one at a time and map each to a token type or a feature. The Schweser-Notes module quiz uses the same shape.

**LO:** CI-7 a: Explain the process of tokenization and describe the fundamental features of tokenized assets and digital ledgers. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a

CI-7 • Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies (IMF, January 2025) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q106 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a; CI notes CI-7 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 a.9)

a.reason: Fails (1) and (3): the conventional bond exists off the ledger, so the token is non-native, and coupons paid by a custodian are not automated on the ledger.

c.reason: Feature swap: restricting transfers to qualified investors is a smart-contract use, which is programmability, not trust.

d.reason: Misdefines migration: migration destroys the original, and a bond kept live off the ledger with a mirror on it is a non-native representation, which fails (1).

questions.question: A lecturer at a Frankfurt business school gives students three situations: (1) the founder of a firm going public knows far more about its prospects than the investors buying its shares; (2) a dealer cannot find a willing buyer for a thinly traded OTC bond; (3) an option buyer holds a right to transact at a future date and the option writer may not perform. Which classification of the three frictions is correct?

options.text: (1) search friction; (2) transaction cost; (3) counterparty risk.
(1) information asymmetry; (2) counterparty risk; (3) search friction.
(1) information asymmetry; (2) search friction; (3) counterparty risk.
(1) information asymmetry; (2) search friction; (3) transaction cost.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Situation (1)**

One party (the founder) has more information than others: information asymmetry. The reading’s own example is a company owner during an IPO.

**Step 2 – Situation (2)**

Diﬀiculty finding a suitable trading partner: search friction.

**Step 3 – Situation (3)**

The risk that one party fails to meet its obligations: counterparty risk. In derivatives it arises at initiation and through the life of the contract, when the buyer holds a future right to transact.

⇒ Information asymmetry, search friction, counterparty risk.

**Interpretation**

Ask what goes wrong: knowing less, not finding a partner, or the partner not performing. Transaction costs are the fees, trading costs and time that every phase carries.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025), Tokenization and Financial Market Ineﬀiciencies; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (2): the founder’s informational edge is asymmetry, and the missing buyer is a search problem.

b.reason: Sibling swap on (2) and (3): the missing buyer is a search friction, and the writer’s possible failure is counterparty risk.

d.reason: Sibling swap on (3): non-performance by the writer is counterparty risk, not a fee or trading cost.

questions.question: A consultant at a Johannesburg exchange maps market frictions to the phases of an asset’s lifecycle, following the IMF note’s lifecycle figure. Which statement is consistent with that mapping?

options.text: Servicing and redemption carry only transaction costs; counterparty risk sits at exchange, information asymmetry at issuance.
Counterparty risk is the main friction at servicing, because coupon and dividend payments can fail once the asset is held.
Information asymmetry sits at exchange, where buyers know less than sellers, while issuance carries transaction costs only.
Search frictions arise only at exchange, because finding a counterparty matters only once an asset has started trading on a market.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the figure**

Issuance: information asymmetry, search frictions, transaction costs. Exchange: search frictions, transaction costs, counterparty risk. Servicing: transaction costs. Redemption: transaction costs.

**Step 2 – Check the description of servicing**

The reading describes servicing and redemption frictions as transaction costs: collecting and transmitting interest, principal and dividend payments, and keeping owner records up to date.

⇒ Three, three, one, one.

**Interpretation**

The uneven load explains where the reading’s tokenization benefits are richest: issuance and trading get several fixes each, servicing and redemption get one, payment automation.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025), lifecycle figure as redrawn in the class notes (Figure CI-7.2); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Figure CI-7.2) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.2)

b.reason: Phase swap: counterparty risk is placed at exchange; the servicing friction is transaction costs.

c.reason: Phase swap: information asymmetry sits at issuance (the IPO example), and issuance carries three frictions, not one.

d.reason: Scope error: the figure places search frictions at issuance as well as at exchange, and SchweserNotes says frictions can arise at any stage.

questions.question: A clearing member defaults on a large derivatives position cleared through a central counterparty (CCP). A risk manager at another clearing member asks how the IMF note describes the CCP’s role. Which description is correct?

options.text: The CCP, acting as a central securities depository, records the default and leaves the loss with the defaulter’s original counterparty.
The CCP covers the default first from its own guarantee fund, and only then draws on the defaulting member’s margin and collateral.
The CCP limits information asymmetry by doing due diligence on members, but it does not stand between the parties to a trade.
The CCP stands between both sides and covers the default from the defaulter’s margin and collateral, then its guarantee fund.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a CCP is**

A CCP is a subcategory of central clearinghouses. It interposes itself as the counterparty to all trading parties in a derivatives contract.

**Step 2 – How it absorbs a default**

It covers nonpayment or nondelivery using the defaulting party’s margin and collateral and, if needed, the CCP’s guarantee fund.

⇒ The defaulter’s own resources go first; the guarantee fund is the backstop.

**Interpretation**

This is the traditional answer to counterparty risk, and it carries fees. CI-7 b.8 and b.10 show why tokenized markets may still need a CCP or locked collateral.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q112 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.3)

a.reason: Role misassignment: CSDs manage settlement; the CCP’s defining act is inter-posing itself between the parties, so the loss does not stay with the original counterparty.

b.reason: Waterfall reversed: the defaulter’s margin and collateral are used first, the guarantee fund only if needed.

c.reason: Role misassignment: due diligence against information asymmetry is the investment bank’s role, and standing between the parties is exactly what a CCP does.

questions.question: A policy adviser at a finance ministry is classifying three cases: (1) a large bank takes excessive risk because it expects a government bailout, keeping the profits and sharing the losses; (2) a retail investor buys a complex product whose risks she does not understand; (3) a custodian charges above-market fees because clients find switching to a rival too costly. Which classification is correct?

options.text: (1) internality; (2) negative externality; (3) market power.
(1) negative externality; (2) internality; (3) market power.
(1) market power; (2) internality; (3) negative externality.
(1) negative externality; (2) market power; (3) internality.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Case (1)**

Excessive risk-taking in expectation of a bailout, with profits kept and losses shared, is moral hazard: the reading’s example of a negative externality, because the losses land on others.

**Step 2 – Case (2)**

Acting against one’s own best interest, such as trading without understanding the risks, is an internality.

**Step 3 – Case (3)**

Above-market fees sustained by switching barriers is market power.

⇒ Others harmed, self harmed, users overcharged.

**Interpretation**

Who bears the cost separates the three: an externality falls on others, an internality on the actor, and market power on the customers who pay the price set.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (2): moral hazard harms others (externality); the investor’s mistake harms herself (internality).

c.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (3): bailout-driven risk-taking is moral hazard, a negative externality, and switching-barrier fees are market power.

d.reason: Sibling swap on (2) and (3): the investor’s mistake is an internality, and the custodian’s fees are market power.

questions.question: The treasurer of a small Nordic utility is considering its first bond issue in tokenized form, similar to the bond BNP Paribas issued in 2022. Which benefit of tokenized issuance is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The token removes the need for due diligence and underwriting, because a shared ledger eliminates information asymmetry.
Tokenized issuance raises registrars’ economies of scale, because registrars and trust companies can handle larger volumes.
Embedding the term sheet and ESG data in the token adds transparency, most useful where issuances are small.
Embedding key data in the token mainly helps the largest issuers, whose information is hardest for investors to obtain.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The issuance benefits**

A shared, programmable ledger links assets directly to owners’ accounts, removing separate recordkeeping and stand-alone custody; smart contracts automate processes such as share auctions; and key data can be embedded in the token.

**Step 2 – Who gains most from embedded data**

Embedding data makes asset and company information easier to access, which is particularly valuable for smaller issuances, where such information is often limited. BNP Paribas’s 2022 tokenized bond embedded its term sheet and ESG data.

⇒ A small utility is the kind of issuer the reading has in mind.

**Interpretation**

Embedded data attacks information asymmetry at issuance by making information easier to reach. The reading does not say it replaces the due diligence and underwriting of investment banks.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q114 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.5)

a.reason: Overreach: the reading says embedded data increases transparency, not that it eliminates information asymmetry or the need for due diligence and underwriting.

b.reason: Polarity flip: economies of scale are the advantage of the traditional intermediaries; the tokenized ledger removes the need for separate recordkeeping.

d.reason: Size reversed: embedded data is most valuable for smaller issuances, where information is often limited.

questions.question: The head of post-trade at a Singapore exchange explains to the board why a tokenized market could settle trades as soon as the parties agree, which the exchange’s current market cannot do. Which explanation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: A CCP on the ledger guarantees every trade from its fund at once; clearinghouses must first collect margin from both sides of every trade.
A smart contract extends intraday credit to whichever party is slower; clearinghouses must wait for both parties to post funds in full.
A shared ledger removes search frictions; in the current market most settlement delay comes from finding a counterparty after the trade.
A smart contract executes only once both cash and securities are locked in; clearinghouses need time to update multiple ledgers.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The tokenized mechanism**

A self-executing smart contract completes a trade only if both the buyer’s cash and the seller’s securities are locked in, so the two legs move together: simultaneous or even instantaneous settlement.

**Step 2 – Why the current market cannot match it**

Instantaneous settlement is not possible in traditional markets because CCHs need time to coordinate and update multiple ledgers.

⇒ One shared ledger with conditional execution replaces several ledgers that must be reconciled.

**Interpretation**

The benefit is lower costs and shorter transaction times, and it can improve liquidity and capital allocation. It does not cover obligations that run past the settlement step (CI-7 b.8).

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q115 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.6)

a.reason: Role misassignment: speed comes from conditional execution on a shared ledger, not from a CCP’s guarantee fund.

b.reason: Invented mechanism: the smart contract locks both legs; it does not lend to the slower party.

c.reason: Phase swap: search frictions concern finding a counterparty before a trade is agreed, not settling it afterwards.

questions.question: A dealer at a London bank trades an OTC product in which information and liquidity are limited. The platform operator proposes moving trading onto a single shared, programmable ledger to which all participants have direct access. Which outcome is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Counterparties become easier to find and costs such as bid-ask spreads fall, so the need for broker-dealers declines.
Search frictions are unchanged, because OTC prices are already centralised, but counterparty risk is fully eliminated.
Reliance on broker-dealers rises, because participants need dealers to interpret the information now held on the ledger.
Bid-ask spreads widen, because the dealers that provided liquidity are disintermediated and lose the incentive to quote.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The OTC friction**

Search frictions bite hardest in OTC markets, where information and liquidity are limited.

**Step 2 – What a single shared ledger does**

Direct access to a single shared ledger makes it easier to find trading counterparties and helps lower costs such as bid-ask spreads, which reduces the need for broker-dealers.

⇒ Sharedness turns a search problem into a visibility problem that the ledger solves.

**Interpretation**

CI-7 c develops the same move as a network externality: as liquidity grows, spreads narrow and more users join. Note what the option does not claim: counterparty risk is not fully removed.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q117 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.7)

b.reason: False premise and overreach: OTC information is limited, not centralised, and counterparty risk is never fully eliminated (between initiation and execution it survives).

c.reason: Polarity flip: the need for broker-dealers falls.

d.reason: Polarity flip: spreads narrow; the reading links the shared ledger to lower bid-ask spreads.

questions.question:
(correction box)

A derivatives risk manager at a Chicago trading firm is assessing how far smart contracts on a programmable ledger can reduce counterparty risk. In which of the following trades would programmability be LEAST effective at mitigating counterparty risk?

options.text: A spot bond trade in which the contract executes only once both the cash and the bonds have been locked in.
A forward contract with delivery long after initiation, in which neither party locks up any collateral.
A cross-currency trade completed in several linked steps, each of them automated by a smart contract.
An option contract in which the writer’s collateral stays locked in the smart contract for its full life.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where programmability works**

A smart contract reduces counterparty risk at the settlement step by completing the trade only when both legs are locked in (A), and it reduces counterparty risk in multistep trades such as cross-currency trades (C).

**Step 2 – Where it cannot reach**

Tokenization cannot fully eliminate counterparty risk when a party fails between contract initiation and execution. The fixes are a CCP or collateral locked up for the duration of the contract (D has that).

**Step 3 – Find the uncovered case**

The forward contract has a long gap between initiation and delivery and no locked collateral.

⇒ Programmability alone cannot manage that exposure.

**Interpretation**

The residual risk is about time: obligations that run past the settlement step (see the correction box). The forward contract is the only option with such a gap and no safeguard.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b and Module Quiz 106.1

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b (Module Quiz 106.1 shape); CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.8)

a.reason: Effective case: locking cash and bonds before execution is the reading’s own example of a self-executing smart contract.

c.reason: Effective case: the reading says smart contracts can reduce counterparty risk in multistep transactions such as cross-currency trades.

d.reason: Effective case: collateral locked for the life of the contract is one of the two fixes the reading names for the residual risk.

questions.question: The head of corporate actions at a custodian bank asks what a programmable ledger would change in the servicing and redemption phase of a tokenized security. Which statement is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: It automates interest and principal, but dividends still need an off-ledger decision, so dividend distribution cannot be embedded.
Its main benefit at this stage is lower search frictions, because holders can find buyers more easily before the asset is redeemed.
It can specify when payments are due and how much to pay per token, and can embed dividend decisions, cutting servicing costs.
It adds a second, on-ledger record of owners beside the registrar’s, which raises recordkeeping costs but makes payments accurate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The servicing friction**

Servicing and redemption carry transaction costs: collecting and transmitting interest, principal and dividend payments, and keeping owner records up to date.

**Step 2 – The tokenized fix**

A shared, programmable ledger automates these payments through smart contracts, linking assets directly to owners. It can specify when payments are due and how much to pay per token, and can even embed dividend distribution decisions.

⇒ Lower servicing costs, with the paying logic in the code.

**Interpretation**

Servicing is the phase with the simplest story: one friction (transaction costs) and one fix (payment automation).

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q120 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.9)

a.reason: Scope error: the reading says dividend distribution decisions can be embedded.

b.reason: Phase swap: lower search frictions are a trading-phase benefit, not a servicing one.

d.reason: Polarity flip: linking assets directly to owners removes the need for separate recordkeeping, so recordkeeping costs fall.

questions.question: A tokenized derivatives venue in Paris decides that collateral for every contract will be locked up on the ledger for the full life of the contract. The venue’s head of risk is asked to describe the trade-off. Which description is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Counterparty risk is mitigated, but locked collateral creates opportunity costs that may discourage investors from trading.
Counterparty risk and transaction costs both fall to zero, because the smart contract now covers the whole period before execution.
Counterparty risk rises, because concentrating all collateral on one ledger creates a single point of failure for the venue.
Counterparty risk is mitigated, and participation rises, because investors prefer contracts whose collateral cannot be withdrawn early.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the rule fixes**

Requiring collateral to be locked up for the duration of the contract is one of the two ways the reading names for mitigating counterparty risk between initiation and execution (the other is a CCP).

**Step 2 – What it costs**

Locking up assets as collateral creates opportunity costs and may discourage investors from using tokenized trades.

⇒ One friction falls (counterparty risk) and another rises (transaction costs, as opportunity cost).

**Interpretation**

This is the clearest case in this LO of a tokenized design both mitigating and increasing frictions at once, which is what the LO wording asks you to explain.

**LO:** CI-7 b: Describe frictions and ineﬀiciencies that can arise during different phases of an asset’s lifecycle and explain how the different features of tokenization can both increase and mitigate risks related to these frictions. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b

CI-7 • Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies (IMF, January 2025) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b; CI notes CI-7 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 b.10)

b.reason: Absolute claim: locked collateral carries an opportunity cost, so transaction costs do not fall to zero.

c.reason: Sibling swap: a single point of failure is the infrastructure externality of a dominant ledger (CI-7 c), not the effect of collateral lock-up on counterparty risk.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the reading says locked collateral creates opportunity costs that may discourage investors from using tokenized trades, not that it draws them in.

questions.loText: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects.
questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (correction box)
questions.question: A financial stability analyst at the European Central Bank is assessing how widespread tokenized bond issuance could affect systemic risk. Which chain of effects is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Debt becomes cheaper to issue, firms replace bank loans with bonds, and bank leverage falls, which reduces the risk of contagion.
Debt becomes cheaper to issue than conventional bonds, borrowing grows more attractive, and higher leverage can raise instability.
Debt becomes costlier to issue because of security spending, borrowing falls, and lower leverage slows the spread of shocks.
Equity becomes cheaper to issue relative to debt, firms shift toward equity funding, and lower leverage dampens shock transmission.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The cost effect**

Tokenization can lower the issuance cost of debt compared with conventional bonds.

**Step 2 – The behavioural effect**

Cheaper debt makes borrowing more attractive and can encourage higher leverage.

**Step 3 – The stability effect**

In a highly interconnected system, higher leverage raises the risk of instability if institutions take on excessive debt.

⇒ Cheaper debt, more borrowing, more leverage, more fragility.

**Interpretation**

This is the channel the SchweserNotes module quiz names first for a highly interconnected market. Leverage was already a traditional amplifier: highly leveraged institutions keep the upside and shift losses onto others. Tokenization feeds it by making debt cheaper.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025), Tokenization and Financial Market Ineﬀiciencies; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c and Module Quiz 106.2

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (correction box) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.1)

a.reason: Invented chain with a polarity flip: the reading says cheaper debt encourages higher leverage, not lower.

c.reason: Polarity flip: tokenization lowers the issuance cost of debt. Security spending is the infrastructure externality, a separate channel.

d.reason: Misreads the channel (see the correction box): the reading’s mechanism is cheaper debt issuance, which raises leverage.

questions.subject: Current Issues
questions.loText: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects.
questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q122 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c
questions.question: The treasurer of a Spanish retail bank asks how the spread of tokenization could change the bank’s funding. Which outcome is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Retail deposits rise as tokenized deposits become more attractive, so the bank can rely less on wholesale funding.
Retail deposits fall, but the bank becomes more stable, because wholesale funding is less prone than deposits to run in stress.
Retail deposits are unaffected, because tokenization changes how securities settle rather than where households keep funds.
Retail deposits fall as funds move into financial assets, so the bank leans on wholesale funding that can dry up in stress.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where retail money goes**

Tokenization makes it easier for retail investors to place funds in financial assets outside traditional bank deposits, so banks may see retail deposits decline.

**Step 2 – What replaces it**

Banks become more reliant on wholesale funding.

**Step 3 – Why that matters**

Wholesale funding can dry up quickly in market stress, raising the risk of defaults and spillovers across the system.

⇒ Deposits out, wholesale in, fragility up.

**Interpretation**

This channel works through funding liquidity, one of the three traditional amplifiers (Figure 1). It is a bank funding effect, distinct from the broker effects of CI-7 d.

questions.question: A supervisor at a securities regulator finds that investors on a shared, programmable ledger hold complex products linked to other assets and to assets pegged to different currencies, with the same collateral reused across several transactions. Which concern does the reading attach to this setting?

options.text: Rehypothecation and quick, cheap movement of funds across linked assets mean a fall in one asset can set off rapid selloffs in several markets.
Fractionalisation of the linked products concentrates retail portfolios in single assets, so that losses remain with the investors who bought them.
Reusing collateral across transactions is escrow certification, so each product is backed by an original asset locked on a separate ledger.
Linked products slow the transmission of shocks, because losses on one asset are offset by gains on the assets to which it is pegged.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the practice**

Collateral reused across multiple transactions is rehypothecation, a feature of the complex products that shared, programmable ledgers make easier to reach.

**Step 2 – Name the risk**

As more investors move funds quickly and cheaply across linked assets and markets, shocks spread more rapidly: a sudden drop in one asset could trigger rapid selloffs in several markets.

⇒ The same interconnectedness that improves access speeds up contagion, and makes it harder for regulators to respond.

**Interpretation**

This channel works through interconnectedness. Note the combination the reading stresses: linked assets, reused collateral, and fast, cheap movement of funds.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q123 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.3)

b.reason: Sibling swap: fractionalisation helps retail investors diversify (a network-externality point); it does not describe linked products or reused collateral.

c.reason: Sibling swap: escrow certificates belong to the common ledger model (CI-7 e); reusing collateral is rehypothecation.

d.reason: Polarity flip: linked assets let shocks spread more rapidly; the reading describes no offsetting effect.

questions.question: A market surveillance oﬀicer at an Australian regulator reviews an episode in which prices on a tokenized market fell sharply within a few minutes. Which explanation and implication are most consistent with the reading?

options.text: An operational failure at the dominant ledger’s single point of failure halted trading, so the fall reflects underinvestment.
Smart contracts pause automatically in volatile markets, so the fall must reflect human order-entry errors rather than automated trading.
A chain of self-executing smart contracts set off large volumes of trades, and faster execution makes such shocks harder to contain.
Fragmentation across non-interoperable ledgers caused the fall, and merging the ledgers would let liquidity flow between the pools.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The mechanism**

Programmable ledgers allow automated trading at much faster speeds. Smart contracts using rules-based algorithms can execute trades instantly or nearly instantly and bundle complex transactions. A chain of self-executing smart contracts that triggers large volumes of trades can contribute to a flash crash.

**Step 2 – The implication**

Faster transaction speeds make it more diﬀicult for policymakers to contain the costs of such externalities.

⇒ Automation explains the speed of the fall, and speed explains why containment is harder.

**Interpretation**

Programmability is a benefit in CI-7 b and a risk here: same feature, opposite sign.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q124 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap: a single point of failure is the infrastructure externality; the reading’s account of a sharp, fast fall is a chain of self-executing smart contracts.

b.reason: Invented property: nothing in the reading says smart contracts pause in volatility; they execute as coded, and chained execution is the reading’s mechanism.

d.reason: Sibling swap: fragmentation is a network-externality problem that reduces liquidity; it is not the reading’s account of rapid price falls.

questions.question: A board member of the private company that operates a dominant tokenized ledger argues that spending on operational security is “our own business decision, with no consequences for anyone else”. Which response best reflects the reading?

options.text: The board member is right: the impact of a failure falls as more users join, because a larger ledger spreads losses more thinly.
The board member is wrong: underinvestment creates risks for every participant, and one point of failure could disrupt the market.
The board member is right: automation removes human and software errors, so the only remaining risk is fraud borne by the operator.
The board member is wrong: security spending is a knowledge externality, because rival ledgers can copy the operator’s code for free.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who bears the risk**

If private operators underinvest in operational security, the resulting risks can affect all participants. A single point of failure in a dominant ledger could disrupt the entire market.

**Step 2 – Why it grows with scale**

The potential impact of failures grows with the number of users and interconnected transactions, so operators must spend more to mitigate operational failures and cyberattacks.

⇒ The operator decides the spending, but everyone bears the failure: an externality.

**Interpretation**

Concentration adds to it: a widely used ledger becomes a target for cyberattacks, with potential disruption across the financial system.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q125 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the impact of failures grows, not shrinks, as users and linked transactions increase.

c.reason: Scope error: the reading lists human and software errors, fraud and system failures, and the risks fall on all participants.

d.reason: Sibling swap: knowledge externalities concern innovation spread through open code, not the spillover from security underinvestment.

questions.question: A junior economist at a central bank writes that because network effects on a tokenized ledger are a positive externality, participation will reach the socially optimal level without any policy action. Which correction is most accurate?

options.text: Even positive externalities can be ineﬀicient: liquidity improves as users join, yet participation may stay below the social optimum.
Network effects on tokenized ledgers are negative, because each new user adds congestion, so participation tends to exceed the optimum.
Network effects are an internality, because each user’s decision to join affects only that user’s own liquidity, so no optimum applies.
The economist is right, because each new user raises liquidity for all users, which gives every potential user a private reason to join.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The definition**

Externalities can be positive or negative, but even positive externalities can lead to socially inefficient outcomes.

**Step 2 – The network case**

Network effects are the reading’s example: liquidity improves as more participants join, yet the number of participants may still remain below the socially optimal level.

⇒ Positive is not the same as optimal.

**Interpretation**

The benefit a new user brings to others does not enter that user’s own decision, which is why participation can fall short.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.b and 106.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q119 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.b and 106.c; CI notes CI-7 b, c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip: network effects are the reading’s example of a positive externality.

c.reason: Sibling swap: an internality is a participant acting against its own interest; network effects spill over to others.

d.reason: Keeps the economist’s error: a private reason to join exists, but the reading says participation may still fall short of the social optimum.

questions.question: Several banks in one region each launch their own tokenized bond ledger, without coordination and with no regulatory requirement for interoperability. A regional regulator’s economist is asked for the most likely consequence. Which outcome is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Shock transmission is amplified, because fragmented ledgers tie institutions together more tightly and speed up the spread of losses.
Programmability falls on each ledger, because smart contracts can run only where one ledger serves the whole of the market.
Liquidity improves, because competition among the ledgers deepens each pool and narrows bid-ask spreads on every platform.
Liquidity splits into segmented pools, search frictions and transaction costs rise, and network externalities weaken.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The condition**

The strength of network externalities depends on the interoperability of ledgers. Multiple non-interoperable ledgers leave users with access only to segmented pools of assets.

**Step 2 – The consequences**

Liquidity can decline, and fragmentation raises transaction costs and search frictions, weakening the benefits of network effects. The risk is greater when private entities set up ledgers without coordination or without regulatory requirements for interoperability.

⇒ Fragmentation lowers sharedness and market eﬀiciency.

**Interpretation**

Fragmentation attacks the liquidity step of the network cycle (Figure 2). SchweserNotes adds that fragmentation does not amplify shock transmission and is unrelated to programmability.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c and Module Quiz 106.2

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q129 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: shock amplification comes from speed, leverage, deposit migration, linked assets and automated trading. Fragmentation reduces liquidity; it is not a transmission channel.

b.reason: Sibling swap: programmability depends on ledger design, not on interoperability.

c.reason: Polarity flip: segmentation reduces liquidity and raises costs.

questions.question: The head of a retail wealth platform tells clients that tokenization will, for the first time, allow small investors to buy fractional shares. Which statement is the most accurate correction?

options.text: On tokenized ledgers, fractional ownership is still limited to equities, so the gain for small investors is lower fees, not wider access.
Fractionalisation raises intermediary risk for small investors, because tokens issued by the issuer add a layer between investor and asset.
Some intermediaries already offer fractional shares of certain equities; tokenization extends this to more assets, including bonds.
The claim is right, but fractionalisation leaves small investors less diversified, which is the internality that the reading warns about.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What already exists**

Some intermediaries already offer fractional shares of certain equities, so fractional ownership is not new.

**Step 2 – What tokenization adds**

Tokenization enables fractionalisation across a wider range of assets, including equities and bonds. When the issuer issues the tokens, intermediary risks can be reduced or even eliminated, improving access particularly for smaller investors.

⇒ The novelty is breadth, not existence.

**Interpretation**

Fractionalisation sits under network externalities because wider participation feeds liquidity. The retail downside (internalities) is CI-7 d.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c and 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q128 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.8)

a.reason: Scope error: tokenization widens fractionalisation beyond equities, to bonds among others.

b.reason: Polarity flip: tokens issued directly by the issuer can reduce or eliminate intermediary risks.

d.reason: Two errors: fractional shares are not new, and fractionalisation helps investors diversify. Insuﬀicient diversification is the reading’s consequence of bypassing advisers (CI-7 d), not of fractionalisation.

questions.question: A venture investor is considering a start-up that builds smart-contract applications on an open-code tokenized ledger, and asks how the reading views knowledge externalities. Which statement is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Knowledge externalities shrink as the ledger’s user base grows, because more users mean more competitors copying each application.
Open code lets others build on existing smart contracts at low or no cost, but easy copying weakens the incentive to fund R&D.
Smart contracts are immutable and so cannot be copied, which means open code strengthens the incentive to invest in R&D.
Licensing and patenting widen the benefits of open-source development, because protected code can be shared more freely.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The positive side**

Because tokenization supports open code development, innovators can build on existing smart contracts and applications at low or no cost, creating wider benefits for users. These knowledge externalities grow as the number of platform users increases.

**Step 2 – The negative side**

Open code access lowers the incentive for significant R&D, because code can be quickly copied and improved by others. Incentives may hold up only if the shared user base is large enough.

⇒ One property, copyable code, produces both effects.

**Interpretation**

The start-up gains from building cheaply on others’ code, and others gain from its code. Patents protect, at the cost of open-source benefits.

**LO:** CI-7 c: Explain how the use of tokenization and digital ledgers can impact financial market externalities, including those related to the transmission of shocks across the financial system, investments in market infrastructure, and network and knowledge effects. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c

CI-7 • Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies (IMF, January 2025) • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q130 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c; CI notes CI-7 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 c.9)

a.reason: Polarity flip: knowledge externalities grow as the user base grows.

c.reason: Misuses immutability: deployed smart contracts are immutable, but open code can still be copied and improved, which is the source of the weaker incentive.

d.reason: Polarity flip: licensing and patenting protect innovations but limit open-source benefits.

questions.question: A consumer protection oﬀicial at a European securities regulator is reviewing a tokenized platform that lets retail investors trade complex assets and derivatives directly, without an adviser. Which assessment is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The main risk is a negative externality, because retail losses on the platform spill over to the other investors who trade the same assets.
The risk is small, because the ledger verifies each trade at once and so stops investors from entering trades whose risks they do not understand.
Direct access can amplify internalities, and the risk of large, sudden losses is greatest where consumer financial protections are weak.
The main risk is market power, because retail investors who bypass advisers are charged higher fees by the platform for complex products.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the inefficiency**

Tokenized ledgers that let retail investors trade directly can amplify internalities: decisions that are not in the investor’s own best interest, such as trading securities whose risks they do not fully understand, especially after bypassing advisers to avoid fees.

**Step 2 – The consequences and the condition**

Insuﬀicient diversification and exposure to large, sudden losses from risky or complex assets and derivatives, especially in the absence of strong consumer financial protections.

⇒ The harm falls on the investor, and weak protections make it worse.

**Interpretation**

For the oﬀicial, the strength of consumer financial protections is the condition that decides how large losses get.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025), Tokenization and Financial Market Ineﬀiciencies; Schweser-Notes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q137 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the loss falls on the investor who made the decision, which is an internality, not a spillover to others.

b.reason: Confuses verification with protection: an immediately verifiable record confirms the trade, not that the investor understood its risks.

d.reason: Sibling swap: market power is about a dominant entity charging above-market fees; the reading’s retail concern here is the investor’s own decisions.

questions.question: A research analyst at an Indian wealth manager is asked whether tokenized ledgers will leave retail investors better or worse diversified. Which answer best reflects the reading?

options.text: Either: fractional shares ease diversifying across more assets, but investors who bypass advisers to save fees may end up under-diversified.
Better diversified, because fractional shares across more assets let small investors spread funds widely even without an adviser.
Worse diversified, because direct trading pushes investors into complex products, and fractional shares stay limited to equities.
Neither: diversification depends only on which assets exist, and tokenization changes how assets settle rather than which ones investors can reach.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The diversification benefit**

Tokenized ledgers support fractionalisation, which lets retail investors buy fractional shares and diversify more easily, across a wider range of assets than intermediaries offer today (CI-7 c).

**Step 2 – The diversification risk**

Direct trading can amplify internalities: investors who bypass advisers to avoid fees may trade risks they do not understand, which can result in insuﬀicient diversification (CI-7 d).

⇒ The reading supports both directions; which one dominates depends on how investors use the access.

**Interpretation**

The class notes’ summary fits: cheaper direct access is the benefit, and losing the adviser who screened the risk is the cost.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.c and 106.d

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.c and 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.2)

b.reason: One-sided: fractionalisation helps, but the reading warns that investors who bypass advisers may end up insuﬀiciently diversified.

c.reason: One-sided and a scope error: bypassing advisers can lead to complex, poorly understood trades, but tokenization extends fractional shares beyond equities, to bonds among others.

d.reason: Scope error: the reading links tokenization to which assets retail investors can reach, through fractionalisation and direct trading.

questions.question: A retail investor in the United States wants to move her portfolio to a cheaper broker without selling the securities. A financial journalist uses her case to explain why brokers can keep fees high. Which explanation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Brokers keep fees high because regulators set minimum commissions, so moving to a cheaper broker changes little for the investor.
In-kind transfers are not allowed between brokers, so she must sell the securities and move the cash, and that is what deters switching.
In-kind transfers settle instantly between brokers, so fees reflect the value of the broker’s service rather than a barrier to switching.
Moving the securities themselves may require going through a clearinghouse, which adds delays and complexity and discourages switching.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What an in-kind transfer is**

Moving the securities themselves rather than selling them and moving cash.

**Step 2 – Why it is a barrier**

In the United States an in-kind transfer may require going through a clearinghouse, which adds delays and complexity. Switching is time-consuming and cumbersome, so investors are discouraged from moving.

⇒ Brokers can keep charging higher fees without losing clients.

**Interpretation**

This is the barrier the ledger removes in the first turn of the argument (Figure 1).

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q132 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.3)

a.reason: Invented mechanism: the reading’s explanation is switching friction, not regulated minimum commissions.

b.reason: Scope error: in-kind transfers are possible; the problem is that they may need a clearinghouse and are slow and cumbersome.

c.reason: Polarity flip: in-kind transfers are slow in traditional markets; instant transfer is what a digital ledger offers.

questions.question: The chief executive of a Toronto online broker asks how the spread of distributed ledgers is likely to affect the fees the firm can charge. Which assessment is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Fees can rise, because verifying ownership on a ledger costs more than clearing through a clearinghouse, and clients bear that cost.
Fees face pressure: switching can be instant, no clearinghouse is needed, competition grows, and scale economies may follow.
Fees are unaffected, because switching brokers on a ledger still requires every transfer to be reconciled through a clearinghouse.
Fees rise as participation grows, because brokers lose economies of scale once clients can switch between them instantly.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Switching becomes easy**

On a digital ledger, changing brokers and transferring assets can be instantaneous, because transactions and ownership records are immediately verifiable. These features also remove the need for a clearinghouse, which reduces costs.

**Step 2 – Further sources of lower fees**

Brokers may lower fees under greater competitive pressure, and increased market participation may let them achieve economies of scale.

⇒ The broker’s fee-setting power weakens from several directions at once.

**Interpretation**

Direct trading would add more pressure, limited by the licensed-broker requirement (CI-7 d.5).

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q133 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the ledger removes the clearinghouse and reduces costs.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the ledger removes the clearinghouse step.

d.reason: Polarity flip: wider participation may give brokers economies of scale.

questions.question: A fintech founder pitches a platform on which retail investors buy tokenized assets directly from issuers, and tells prospective investors that “brokers will soon be unnecessary everywhere”. Which response best reflects the reading?

options.text: Direct trading would push brokers to lower fees, but in most countries trading must still be conducted through licensed brokers.
Direct trading would have no effect on broker fees, because issuers selling directly would simply charge the same fees as brokers.
Direct trading would end the internality problem, because retail investors who buy from issuers receive the issuer’s data in the token.
Direct trading is barred in most countries, because issuers are not permitted to create tokens that represent their own securities.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The economic effect**

Direct trading by retail investors, buying assets directly from issuers, would put additional pressure on brokers to lower their fees.

**Step 2 – The legal limit**

In most countries, trading is still required to be conducted through licensed brokers.

⇒ Pressure on fees, yes; brokers unnecessary everywhere, no.

**Interpretation**

The founder’s claim fails on regulation, not on economics: the reading accepts the fee pressure but notes the licensed-broker requirement.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q136 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the reading says direct trading would add pressure on broker fees.

c.reason: Polarity flip: direct access can amplify internalities; embedded data improves transparency (CI-7 b) but does not end self-harming decisions.

d.reason: Invented prohibition: the limit is that trading must go through licensed brokers, not a ban on issuers tokenizing their securities.

questions.loText: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms.
questions.reading: CI-7: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
questions.source: Adapted from CI QB VI Q139 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d
questions.question: A privately owned ledger offered free access at launch and now dominates trading in tokenized bonds. An analyst at a competition authority is asked what the reading implies for the fees users will pay from here. Which assessment is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Fees stay low, because each new participant adds liquidity that lowers the owner’s costs, a positive network externality.
Fees fall as the ledger grows, because the owner gains economies of scale and competitive pressure pushes it to pass the savings on.
Fees can rise as the ledger grows more widely shared and dominant: the owner extracts monopoly rents, a market power ineﬀiciency.
Fees rise only to fund security spending, because underinvestment on a dominant ledger would expose every participant.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The pattern**

A private owner may offer free access while the ledger is new to attract users, then begin charging once the ledger is popular and holds a strong market position.

**Step 2 – The direction of fees**

Private owners may charge high fees, known as monopoly rents, with fees rising as the ledger becomes more widely shared and dominant: a market power ineﬀiciency.

⇒ Dominance first, then rents that grow with it.

**Interpretation**

Network effects help build the dominance; the fee-setting that follows is market power. Scale economies and competition are the reading’s reasons for lower broker fees.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d and Module Quiz 106.2

a.reason: Cause confused with conduct: network effects build the dominance; they do not keep the owner’s fees low.

b.reason: Sibling swap: scale economies and competition explain lower broker fees; a dominant ledger’s fees can rise.

d.reason: Invented justification: the reading’s infrastructure externality concerns underinvestment in security; it does not tie the owner’s fees to security spending.

questions.question: A competition economist is reviewing how the owner of a dominant privately owned ledger uses the trading data it collects from users. Which set of practices does the reading identify as a source of market power ineﬀiciency?

options.text: Publishing central price information to all users, standardising contracts and narrowing bid-ask spreads across the ledger.
Offering credit based on the data, selling the data, and charging higher fees to the most active traders on the ledger.
Paying rebates to the most active traders, sharing data with regulators, and lowering fees as the ledger keeps growing.
Embedding term sheets and ESG data in tokens, so that investors can see issuer information directly on the ledger.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The source of the power**

The owner of a privately owned ledger sees privileged data on its users’ trading.

**Step 2 – The practices**

The reading lists three ways to monetise it: offering credit, selling the data, and charging higher fees to the most active traders.

⇒ Data held by a dominant owner is a second source of market power, alongside fees.

**Interpretation**

Data monetisation sits beside monopoly rents: both are market power of privately owned ledgers.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q135 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: central price information, standard contracts and narrower spreads are network-externality benefits (CI-7 c).

c.reason: Polarity flip: the reading has the most active traders charged more, and fees on a dominant ledger can rise, not fall.

d.reason: Sibling swap: embedding term sheets and ESG data is an issuance benefit (CI-7 b), not a use of users’ trading data.

questions.question: A brokerage strategist writes: “Distributed ledgers remove the switching barriers that let brokers charge high fees, so market power ineﬀiciencies in retail investing will disappear.” Which response best reflects the reading?

options.text: The statement is correct, because once ownership records are immediately verifiable no entity can charge above-market fees.
The statement is wrong, because instant switching covers only cash, so in-kind transfers still need a clearinghouse on a ledger.
The statement is correct, because ledger owners compete for users and so pass on the savings from removing the clearinghouse.
The statement is half right: ledgers can erode brokers’ market power, but a dominant private ledger can create new market power.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The first turn**

On a digital ledger switching brokers can be instantaneous and needs no clearinghouse, which reduces costs and puts pressure on broker fees. The strategist has this part right.

**Step 2 – The second turn**

Privately owned ledgers can introduce new market power ineﬀiciencies: high fees on dominant platforms and monetised privileged data.

⇒ Market power can move from the broker to the ledger owner rather than disappear.

**Interpretation**

The class notes’ argument that turns around twice (Figure 1): stopping at “DLT reduces market power” is half the answer.

**LO:** CI-7 d: Explain how the proliferation of distributed ledger technologies can impact retail investors and brokerage firms. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.d

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.d; CI notes CI-7 d (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 d.8)

a.reason: Absolute claim: verifiable records weaken the brokers’ switching barrier, but a dominant ledger owner can still charge above-market fees.

b.reason: Scope error: on a digital ledger, assets move between brokers instantly, with no clearinghouse.

c.reason: Scope error: privately owned ledgers can create new market power, so savings need not be passed on.
