questions.question: A market infrastructure consultant is classifying three proposals for sharing tokenized assets: (1) all banks and their clients join one system on which every asset is created directly; (2) bonds held on several existing ledgers are placed in escrow and trade on a central ledger as escrow certificates; (3) existing ledgers adopt a standardised technology so that they run the same programs and coordinate transfers. Which classification is correct?

options.text: (1) single ledger; (2) common ledger; (3) compatible ledgers.
(1) single ledger; (2) compatible ledgers; (3) common ledger.
(1) common ledger; (2) single ledger; (3) compatible ledgers.
(1) single-operator system; (2) common ledger; (3) permissionless DLT.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Proposal (1)**

All parties or their intermediaries on one system, with all assets created directly on it: the single ledger model.

**Step 2 – Proposal (2)**

Representations of non-native assets that exist on other ledgers, with the originals in escrow and represented through escrow certificates: the common ledger model.

**Step 3 – Proposal (3)**

Standardised technology that lets different ledgers run the same programs and coordinate transfers: the compatible ledger model.

⇒ One system; one meeting point for many ledgers; one standard for many ledgers.

**Interpretation**

The three are the reading’s ways of achieving sharedness. The class notes read them as a spectrum: sharedness bought with centralisation, with escrow and certificates, or with a standard and no central point.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025), Tokenization and Financial Market Ineﬀiciencies; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.1)

b.reason: Sibling swap on (2) and (3): escrow and certificates define the common ledger; a shared standard defines compatible ledgers.

c.reason: Sibling swap on (1) and (2): one system with all assets created on it is the single ledger; escrowed originals define the common ledger.

d.reason: Axis confusion: single-operator systems and permissionless DLT are trust models, not ways of achieving sharedness.

questions.question: A risk oﬀicer at an asset manager is asked to approve trading a tokenized bond on a common ledger. Which description of what the asset manager would hold is most accurate?

options.text: A native token reissued on the common ledger after the bond is destroyed on its home ledger, so nothing else needs to be relied on.
A copy of the bond that trades freely on both ledgers at once, so the holder can sell on whichever ledger offers the better price.
An escrow certificate for the bond, which stays in escrow on its home ledger, so the holder relies on that escrow too.
A bond on its home ledger that runs the same programs as the common ledger, so transfers are coordinated with no representation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The common ledger mechanism**

Common ledger models allow representations of non-native assets that exist on other ledgers. The original asset is placed in escrow and represented through an escrow certificate.

**Step 2 – What the holder relies on**

The bond stays on its home ledger, locked in escrow; the asset manager holds the certificate that represents it.

⇒ The arrangement adds a second asset, the certificate, and so a second thing that can fail.

**Interpretation**

The class notes make the point: the common ledger is the model that introduces the escrow certificate, and with it a dependence on the escrow behind it. This is the contrast with migration, which leaves no original behind.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.a and 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q142 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.a and 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.2)

a.reason: Sibling swap: destroying the original and reissuing a native token is migration (CI-7 a), not the common ledger model.

b.reason: Scope error: the original is locked in escrow precisely so that it is not traded alongside its representation.

d.reason: Sibling swap: running the same programs and coordinating transfers describes compatible ledgers, which need no escrow certificate.

questions.question: A systems architect at a Tokyo securities firm is contrasting programmability on a digital ledger with the firm’s current set-up. Which contrast is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: On the ledger, users send instructions to a separate database operator; in the current set-up, code and data sit in one system.
On the ledger, code and database are kept apart for security, which makes smart contracts harder to bundle than in the current set-up.
On the ledger, programmability means all relevant parties can reach the same records; the current set-up keeps records apart.
On the ledger, code and database are integrated, so transactions are coherent and eﬀicient and smart contracts are easy to bundle.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The ledger**

Programmability in digital ledgers means the code and the database are integrated within the system.

**Step 2 – The traditional set-up**

External users must send instructions to a separate database operator.

**Step 3 – What integration buys**

Internal programmability ensures transactions are coherent and eﬀicient, and makes it easier to bundle or link smart contracts.

⇒ No external system has to process the transaction.

**Interpretation**

Smart contracts can act on the records directly because code and records live in one place (Figure 2).

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q144 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.3)

a.reason: Mirror reversal: the separate database operator is the traditional set-up, and integration is the ledger.

b.reason: Polarity flip: integration makes bundling easier, not harder.

c.reason: Feature swap: access to the same records by all relevant parties is sharedness, not programmability.

questions.question: A governance consultant at a Swiss bank compares three ways of establishing trust on a ledger: (1) one entity manages the records and executes and confirms transactions; (2) anyone can join, transact and validate, and validators are rewarded; (3) only participants approved by a central entity or consortium can access or validate transactions. Which matching is correct?

options.text: (1) single ledger model; (2) permissionless DLT; (3) permissioned DLT.
(1) single-operator system; (2) permissionless DLT; (3) permissioned DLT.
(1) single-operator system; (2) permissioned DLT; (3) permissionless DLT.
(1) permissioned DLT; (2) permissionless DLT; (3) common ledger model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Design (1)**

One entity manages records and executes and confirms transactions: a single-operator system. Trust rests on the operator’s credibility, supervision and oversight.

**Step 2 – Design (2)**

A decentralised network that anyone can join, transact on and help validate, with validators rewarded: permissionless DLT.

**Step 3 – Design (3)**

Only participants approved by a central entity or consortium can access or validate: permissioned DLT, the hybrid of the other two.

⇒ Centralised, open, and closed group.

**Interpretation**

Each design rests trust on something different, and each fails when that thing fails.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q145 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.4)

a.reason: Axis confusion on (1): the single ledger model is a way of achieving sharedness; one entity running the records is the single-operator trust model.

c.reason: Sibling swap on (2) and (3): open validation with rewards is permissionless; consortium approval is permissioned.

d.reason: Two errors: (1) is the single-operator system, and (3) is permissioned DLT; the common ledger model is a sharedness model.

questions.question: A supervisor at an Asian securities regulator is reviewing a ledger whose validators are a small group of banks certified by a consortium. Which trust failure is this design most exposed to, and what limits it?

options.text: Authorised participants colluding to alter the ledger or its code, limited by reputation and by regulatory oversight and penalties.
An attacker gaining more than 50% of the network’s computing power, limited by the rewards paid to the validators of the network.
Users manipulating transaction fees to front-run others, limited by the consortium certifying each transaction in the queue.
Failure of the single entity that runs the ledger, limited only by its credibility and by the strength of users’ legal protections.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the design**

Validators limited to a small group certified by a consortium: permissioned DLT.

**Step 2 – Its failure**

A permissioned DLT can fail if authorised participants collude to modify the ledger or its programming for their own benefit.

**Step 3 – What limits it**

Participants generally want to protect their reputations to earn future profits, and regulatory oversight and penalties for noncompliance discourage abuse.

⇒ Collusion, checked by reputation and regulation.

**Interpretation**

The structure can also improve security and simplify regulation. Because a permissioned DLT is a hybrid, it can show failures of either design, but collusion is the one the reading attaches to it specifically.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e and Module Quiz 106.2

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q148 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e (Module Quiz 106.2 shape) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.5)

b.reason: Sibling swap: a 50% computing-power attack is the consensus attack on a permissionless proof-of-work ledger.

c.reason: Sibling swap with a misassigned mitigant: fee manipulation is a permissionless weakness, and consortium certification is a permissioned feature.

d.reason: Sibling swap: dependence on a single entity’s credibility and legal protections describes the single-operator system.

questions.question: A cybersecurity analyst at a crypto-asset exchange explains how the consensus mechanism of a permissionless proof-of-work ledger could be compromised. Which condition does the reading identify?

options.text: An attacker acquires more than 50% of the tokens outstanding on the ledger, which gives it a majority of the votes on each block.
An attacker gains a majority of the seats on the consortium that certifies the ledger’s validators and approves its participants.
An attacker obtains the credentials of the single entity that confirms transactions, so that it can alter records undetected.
An attacker gains control of more than 50% of the computing power that is used to validate transactions on the ledger.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why permissionless is exposed**

A permissionless DLT lets anyone participate and validate transactions, so it is vulnerable to attacks that compromise the consensus mechanism.

**Step 2 – The condition**

In a proof-of-work system, the attack can succeed if the attacker gains control of more than 50% of the computing power used to validate transactions.

⇒ Computing power, not token holdings, is the resource that matters in proof of work.

**Interpretation**

The class notes’ “51% attack” label is looser; see the precision note.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q146 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (precision note) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.6)

a.reason: Wrong input twin: the same 50% threshold applied to the wrong resource; the reading’s condition is computing power used to validate.

b.reason: Model confusion: a consortium that certifies validators belongs to permissioned DLT; a permissionless ledger has none.

c.reason: Model confusion: one entity confirming transactions is the single-operator system.

questions.question: A trader on a permissionless ledger notices that her large orders are repeatedly preceded and followed by trades from the same address, which profits at her expense. Which explanation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Rehypothecation: the collateral backing her orders is reused by the other address across several linked transactions.
A sandwich attack: by manipulating transaction fees, the attacker places trades just before and after hers in the queue.
Collusion among authorised validators, who change the ledger’s programming to reorder transactions for their own gain.
A consensus attack: the other address controls more than 50% of computing power and rewrites her trades after validation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The mechanism**

On a permissionless ledger, trust can be undermined if users manipulate transaction fees offered by others, positioning their own trades ahead of others in the validation queue. This enables front running.

**Step 2 – The pattern**

A sandwich attack is a form of front running in which the attacker places transactions before and after a victim’s transaction to generate a profit.

⇒ Trades just before and just after hers, from the same address, at her expense: a sandwich attack.

**Interpretation**

This failure needs no control of the consensus. It exploits the ordering of the validation queue, which is why the reading lists it separately from the 50% attack.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q147 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: rehypothecation is the reuse of collateral across transactions (CI-7 c), not an ordering attack.

c.reason: Model confusion: collusion among authorised validators is the permissioned failure; the trader is on a permissionless ledger.

d.reason: Sibling swap: a 50% computing-power attack compromises consensus itself; the pattern described is queue positioning through fees.

questions.question: The board of a Dubai bank must choose between running a tokenized platform as a single-operator system or as a permissioned DLT with several certified participants. A director argues that the single-operator design carries less risk of trust failure, because one accountable entity is easier to supervise. Which response best reflects the reading?

options.text: The director is right: a single operator has no one to collude with, so its risk of trust failure is lower than a permissioned DLT’s.
The director is right in effect: both designs restrict participation, so the risks are identical and supervision decides the choice.
The director is wrong: risks are similar but higher for one operator, whose trust rests only on its credibility and legal protections.
The director is wrong: permissioned DLT has no trust risk, because reputation and regulatory penalties remove the incentive to collude.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The comparison in the reading**

The risks of trust failure in a fully centralised single-operator system are similar to those in a permissioned DLT.

**Step 2 – The ranking**

They are even higher, because trust in a single-operator system does not rely on consensus among participants and depends entirely on the operator’s credibility and the strength of legal protections.

⇒ Similar in kind, worse in degree.

**Interpretation**

The director’s “one accountable entity” is the reason for the higher risk: everything rides on it, whereas a permissioned DLT needs several participants to collude.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB VI Q149 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 106.e; CI notes CI-7 e (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-7 e.8)

a.reason: True premise, wrong conclusion: a single operator cannot collude, but it fails through its own failure or misuse, and the reading ranks that risk higher.

b.reason: Absolute claim: “identical” contradicts the reading, which ranks single-operator risk higher.

d.reason: Absolute claim: reputation and regulatory oversight help limit collusion in a permissioned DLT; they do not remove the risk of trust failure.

questions.question: A compliance director at a global bank is weighing whether to settle tokenized trades on a permissionless DLT. Beyond attacks on the consensus mechanism and on transaction ordering, which further weaknesses does the reading attribute to this design?

options.text: Collusion among the authorised validators, and reliance on reputational incentives that weaken once validators expect no future profits.
Dependence on one operator’s credibility, and a legal framework that gives users weaker protection than the operator’s own rules.
External information more exposed to cyberattacks with no central authority, and regulatory compliance harder to enforce.
Lower sharedness than a single ledger, because anyone can join, which splits the ledger’s liquidity into segmented validator pools.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Set aside what the stem excludes**

Attacks on consensus (more than 50% of proof-of-work computing power) and on ordering (fee manipulation, front running, sandwich attacks) are already named.

**Step 2 – The remaining permissionless weaknesses**

The absence of a central authority leaves external information more vulnerable to cyberattacks, and the decentralised structure makes regulatory compliance more challenging to enforce.

⇒ Open and headless: no guardian for outside information, no single point for a regulator to act on.

**Interpretation**

The openness that removes the need to trust one operator also removes the party a regulator would hold to account.

**LO:** CI-7 e: Compare different models and methods that are currently available to achieve sharedness, programmability, and trust on a ledger, and describe the conditions under which trust can fail in such models. • **Reference:** IMF Fintech Note (January 2025); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 106, LO 106.e

a.reason: Model confusion: collusion among authorised validators, and the reputational check on it, belong to permissioned DLT.

b.reason: Model confusion: dependence on one operator’s credibility and legal protections is the single-operator system.

d.reason: Axis confusion: open participation is a trust-design feature; segmented liquidity pools come from non-interoperable ledgers (CI-7 c), not from permissionless validation.

questions.loText: Describe characteristics of cyber risks and information/communication technology (ICT) risks faced by financial institutions.
questions.reading: CI-8: Digital Resilience and Financial Stability: The Quest for Policy Tools in the Financial Sector
questions.topic: Digital Resilience and Financial Stability: The Quest for Policy Tools in the Financial Sector
questions.source: New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.a; CI notes CI-8 a
questions.question: The operational risk oﬀicer of a Lisbon-based retail bank is classifying two incidents from the same quarter. In the first, a denial-of-service attack made online banking unavailable for an afternoon. In the second, a failed software upgrade at the bank’s cloud provider made online banking unavailable for an afternoon. Based on the distinction drawn in the Banco de España paper, which classification is correct?

options.text: Both are cyber risk events, because each caused a loss of availability of data systems, and cyber risk is defined by loss of the CIA triad.
The first is a cyber risk event and the second an ICT risk event, because only the first stems from a cyberattack.
Both are ICT risk events, because each disrupted information and communication systems, whatever caused the disruption.
Neither is a cyber risk event unless client information was also breached, because cyber risk concerns the confidentiality of data.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Apply the definitions**

Cyber risk is the loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and data systems that results from a cyberattack. ICT risk is disruption to information and communication systems with similar effects that does not stem from a cyberattack.

**Step 2 – Read the cause, not the effect**

Both incidents had the same effect: online banking was unavailable. The DoS attack is a cyberattack, so it is cyber risk. The failed upgrade is not an attack, so it is ICT risk.

⇒ Same consequence, different cause, different class.

**Interpretation**

The reading’s distinction is about the origin of the event. A customer locked out of online banking cannot tell the two apart, which is exactly why the class must be read from the cause.

**LO:** CI-8 a: Describe characteristics of cyber risks and information/communication technology (ICT) risks faced by financial institutions. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023), Digital Resilience and Financial Stability: The Quest for Policy Tools in the Financial Sector; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.a; CI notes CI-8 a (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 a.1)

a.reason: Classifies by effect: loss of availability is common to both, but only an attack makes it cyber risk. An ICT event may have similar effects by definition.

c.reason: Scope error: ICT risk is the disruption that does not stem from a cyberattack. The DoS attack is the textbook cyber case; DoS attacks are among the reading’s examples of cyber incidents.

d.reason: Scope error: cyber risk covers all three legs of the CIA triad, availability included, not confidentiality alone.

The overwhelming level of digitalisation at financial institutions, combined with the essential nature of their services, places them in a vulnerable position.

questions.question: After migrating its core systems to public cloud providers, a Frankfurt bank’s CRO is preparing a note for the board on how the move has changed the bank’s risk profile. Based on the Banco de España paper, which statement should the note contain?

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The cyber leg**

Financial institutions have strongly embraced cloud computing, and this has brought a corresponding decrease in cyber risks. Cloud service providers are expected to have extremely robust controls in place.

**Step 2 – The ICT leg**

⇒ The bank has exchanged part of one exposure for more of the other.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test the claim of full transfer**

The reading’s main issue with cloud computing is that it moves some, but not all, of an organisation’s cyber risks to the cloud service providers.

**Step 2 – Why the transfer is partial**

The organisation’s own providers and customers might not always have adequate controls. Those weak links stay with the firm, however strong the cloud provider is.

⇒ The provider’s controls do not cover the rest of the firm’s chain.

Strong controls at the provider are an expectation, not a transfer of every exposure. The vendor risk manager has confused the provider’s robustness with the firm’s whole exposure.

questions.question: The chief information oﬀicer of a Zurich wealth manager proposes moving from a single cloud provider to a multicloud set-up. The risk committee asks what, according to the Banco de España paper, the move would buy and what it would cost. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: It removes concentration risk entirely and adds no new risk, because no single provider would hold all of the firm’s computing assets.
It raises the damage a single cyberattack can do, because an attack on one cloud can spread across the firm’s connected clouds.
It limits the damage one cyberattack can do and also tightens stewardship, because each provider oversees a smaller share of the processes.
It limits the damage one cyberattack can do by spreading assets across clouds, at the cost of weaker stewardship over the processes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What multiclouds buy**

Cloud computing has needed to evolve, for example to multiclouds, to deal with concentration risks. Spreading computing assets over multiple clouds rather than one limits the amount of damage a cyberattack could do.

**Step 2 – What they cost**

The evolution comes with unintended additional risks, such as weaker stewardship over the distributed computing processes.

⇒ Less damage from any one attack, less control over the whole.

**Interpretation**

Diversifying the infrastructure buys resilience and costs oversight. The risk committee should expect both in the proposal.

questions.question: The head of a central bank’s financial stability department is setting the scope of a new workstream on cyber risk. Based on the Banco de España paper, which framing should guide the workstream?

**Step 1 – The direction**

The reading names the most important consideration: how technology risks can lead to the realisation of financial risks.

**Step 2 – The financial risks**

Triggered cyber vulnerabilities can cause illiquidity, excessive leverage and loss of customer trust.

⇒ The workstream should start from the technology event and trace it to these three.

**Interpretation**

This is the frame for the whole LO. The CIA triad is the join between the two sides (Figure 1), and contagion and loss of confidence are how the financial effects become systemic.

questions.question: A supervisor at a European national competent authority is ranking three scenarios for a cyber exercise at a large bank: (i) theft of client records, (ii) corruption of the payment ledger so that balances cannot be trusted, and (iii) a prolonged outage of core systems. Using the severity the Banco de España paper associates with each leg of the CIA triad, which ranking is most consistent with the paper?

options.text: Scenarios (ii) and (iii) ahead of (i), because severity tends to be higher for integrity and availability than for confidentiality.
Scenario (i) ahead of (ii) and (iii), because breaches of client confidentiality do the most damage to customers’ trust in the bank.
Scenarios (i) and (ii) ahead of (iii), because an outage leaves the data intact and is ICT risk rather than cyber risk.
All three scenarios equally, because the paper treats the effects of systemic risk on the CIA triad as impossible to rank.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Map each scenario to a leg of the triad**

(i) Theft of client records: confidentiality. (ii) A corrupted ledger whose balances cannot be trusted: integrity. (iii) A prolonged outage of core systems: availability.

**Step 2 – Apply the severity ordering**

Severity seems lower for data confidentiality and higher for data integrity and for the availability of data and systems for operational use.

⇒ Scenarios (ii) and (iii) rank ahead of scenario (i).

**Interpretation**

The ordering is counter-intuitive and is the examinable detail. A bank whose balances cannot be relied on, or whose systems cannot be used, has a harder problem than one whose data have been exposed.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b

c.reason: Severity flip with a classification error: availability is among the more severe legs. Whether an outage is cyber or ICT risk depends on its cause (CI-8 a), and either way it is an availability effect.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the effects are wide-ranging, but the reading does rank them, lower for confidentiality and higher for integrity and availability.

questions.question: A research economist at a central bank proposes to estimate the probability that a cyber incident at one bank spreads to others by extrapolating linearly from past incidents. Which response best reflects the Banco de España paper?

options.text: The approach is sound, because the paper finds that cyber contagion grows in proportion to the number of institutions affected.
The approach is sound in principle, but it should draw on the extensive cyber loss data that financial institutions already report.
Contagion effects are nonlinear, so key events are hard to predict; the paper proposes relying on liquidity buffers instead.
Contagion effects are nonlinear, so key events are hard to predict accurately; the paper proposes agent-based models instead.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why extrapolation fails**

Contagion effects are nonlinear, so it is challenging to predict the probability of key events with reasonable accuracy.

**Step 2 – The reading’s response**

Use agent-based models: computer simulations of the actions and interactions among agents, which quantify a cyber incident’s CIA effects and how they reach institutions’ liquidity and asset values.

⇒ Simulation replaces extrapolation.

**Interpretation**

A linear rule assumes that twice the trigger gives twice the spread. With nonlinear contagion, one key triggering event can spread extremely rapidly, so the past is a poor straight-line guide.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.a and LO 107.b

c.reason: True premise, wrong tool: contagion is nonlinear, but the reading’s answer to the prediction problem is agent-based models. Liquidity buffers help to mitigate cyber-driven runs in theory; they do not estimate the probability of contagion.

The conclusion is misleading only because the blocked withdrawals will all be processed at the bank once its systems are restored.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the surface shows**

A cyber incident triggers a run, but no withdrawals happen because the bank’s systems cannot process transactions. It appears that technology has suppressed the contagion.

**Step 2 – Why that is misleading**

The bank’s customers have other alternatives, such as withdrawing funds they have on deposit with other banks.

⇒ The run is not stopped; it shows up elsewhere.

**Interpretation**

This is the reading’s reason for agent-based models: what appears to happen between technology and finance is not always accurate, and a simulation of agents’ behaviour traces where the pressure goes.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b and LO 107.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q79 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.b; CI notes CI-8 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 b.5)

a.reason: Sibling swap into CI-8 c: a circuit breaker is a deliberate, temporary pause on normal rules and regulations, not a system failure.

b.reason: Polarity flip: triggered cyber vulnerabilities can cause illiquidity and loss of trust, and the run can continue at other banks.

d.reason: Right verdict, wrong reason: the reading’s point is that customers can act through other banks now, not that the blocked withdrawals are only delayed.

questions.question: A supervisor is drafting operational expectations for a banking system in which institutions rely on the same cloud providers, networks and software. She asks what standard of reliability the Banco de España paper implies for each institution. Which answer is most consistent with the paper?

options.text: Each institution should be tested to show it can recover quickly enough from a cyber incident, which need not mean 100% reliability.
Each institution should show 100% reliability, because a single key triggering event in an integrated system is enough to start contagion.
Only the largest cloud providers need to be tested, because individual institutions’ reliability does not affect the continuity of the system.
Each institution should be tested against cyberattacks only, because ICT disruptions that do not stem from attacks do not threaten continuity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why every institution matters**

Virtually all financial institutions are digitalised and have become integrated and more reliant on each other through cloud computing, networks and shared software.

**Step 2 – The standard**

Each participating institution must be reliable enough to recover quickly from a cyber incident, to keep key functions of the financial system running. Each must be tested to ensure it is suﬀiciently reliable, which does not necessarily mean 100% reliability.

⇒ Quick recovery, tested, short of perfection.

**Interpretation**

The standard is about continuity of the system’s key functions. It does not ask any institution to be immune; it asks each to come back fast.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q80 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.b; CI notes CI-8 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 b.6)

b.reason: Absolute claim: suﬀicient reliability does not necessarily mean 100%. The premise about one key triggering event is true, but it does not imply perfection.

c.reason: Scope error: the reading requires each participating institution to be tested, because all are interdependent.

d.reason: Scope error: each institution must be tested given the importance of ICT functions in the financial system, and ICT disruptions such as physical outages are a key concern (CI-8 a). Testing cannot stop at cyberattacks.

questions.question: The treasurer of a bank proposes to size a liquidity buffer against cyber-driven deposit runs by studying how often such buffers have been drawn on in past episodes. Which comment is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: The approach is sound, because buffers against cyber-driven runs have often been drawn on, which gives a long history to calibrate from.
The approach is flawed, because the paper finds that liquidity buffers do not help to mitigate cyber-driven runs, even in theory.
The approach is flawed, because the paper replaces liquidity buffers with circuit breakers as the tool against cyber-driven runs.
The approach is flawed: buffers help in theory, but ample system liquidity has meant they have not been used; use agent-based models.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Buffers in theory**

Building up liquidity buffers helps to mitigate the effects of bank runs caused by cyber shocks, in theory.

**Step 2 – Buffers in history**

There has been a high level of liquidity in the financial system for a reasonable amount of time, so such buffers have not had to be used.

**Step 3 – What to use instead**

A more accurate assessment of the impact of a loss of confidence requires agent-based models.

⇒ There is no record of drawdowns to calibrate from; simulation fills the gap.

**Interpretation**

The treasurer’s method needs a history that does not exist. The idea of a buffer is sound; the calibration has to come from modelling the loss of confidence.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.b; CI notes CI-8 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 b.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the buffers have not had to be used, because system liquidity has been high.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the theory: the reading says buffers do help mitigate cyber-driven runs in theory.

c.reason: Sibling swap into CI-8 c: the reading says buffers do help in theory, and circuit breakers supplement existing deposit controls; nothing in the reading has them replace buffers.

questions.question: Several banks in one country run their core systems on the same software from a single vendor. A financial stability analyst is asked how a cyber incident at one of the banks could spread. Which assessment is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: Contagion is unlikely, because highly integrated connections give the system redundant pathways that slow the spread of a shock.
Highly integrated connections open the way to significant contagion, which can spread extremely rapidly from one key trigger.
Contagion needs several simultaneous triggering events, so a single incident at one bank is likely to stay within that bank.
Contagion is possible, but its probability can be predicted accurately from the number of banks that share the vendor’s software.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Integration**

The modern design of cyber and ICT connections is highly integrated, which opens the potential for significant contagion effects. Shared software is one of the links that make institutions reliant on each other.

**Step 2 – Speed and trigger**

Financial contagion can occur extremely rapidly through the industry with the onset of just one key triggering event.

⇒ One incident at one bank can be enough.

**Interpretation**

The vendor in the stem is a shared node. The reading’s point is that integration raises the potential for contagion, not that it adds redundancy.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q81 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.b; CI notes CI-8 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 b.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip: high integration opens the potential for contagion rather than slowing it.

c.reason: Scope error: one key triggering event is enough.

d.reason: Polarity flip on predictability: contagion effects are nonlinear, so the probability of key events is hard to predict with reasonable accuracy.

questions.question: In a speech, a deputy governor describes where the chain from cyber and ICT risks to systemic financial risk ends. Which statement is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: It ends in higher operational losses at the institutions hit, a channel the paper treats as separate from the deposit runs of past crises.
It ends in a system-wide loss of data confidentiality, because client data are the asset most severely affected by cyber incidents.
It ends in an overwhelming loss of customer confidence, which in the past has often shown up as runs driven by panic or fundamentals.
It ends in concentration at a few cloud providers, which then become systemically important technological institutions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The end point**

The ultimate result of cyber and ICT risks, combined with the vulnerabilities of financial institutions, is an overwhelming loss of customer confidence.

**Step 2 – The precedent**

The combination has often been seen in the past, in runs on bank deposits that stemmed from customer panic or financial fundamentals.

⇒ A cyber shock ends in the familiar way, as a run.

**Interpretation**

The first macroprudential tool in CI-8 c, the circuit breaker, is aimed at exactly this run. The class notes put it the same way: cyber risks can diminish customer confidence, potentially leading to bank runs and systemic instability.

**LO:** CI-8 b: Assess the interactions between cyber and ICT risks and financial risks and explain how cyber and ICT risk events at financial institutions can lead to systemic financial risk. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.b

CI-8 • Digital Resilience and Financial Stability: The Quest for Policy Tools in the Financial Sector (Banco de España, April 2023) • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.b; CI notes CI-8 b (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 b.9)

a.reason: Scope error: the reading ties the end point to loss of confidence and runs of the familiar kind, not to a separate channel of operational losses.

b.reason: Severity flip: confidentiality is the leg with the lower severity, so it is not the end point of the chain.

d.reason: Sibling swap into CI-8 c: systemically important technological institutions are the target of structural measures, not the end point of the chain from cyber risk to systemic risk.

questions.question: A policy adviser at a finance ministry is drafting a national digital resilience strategy around the Banco de España paper’s two-part approach. Which description of the two parts is correct?

options.text: Framework policies give operational guidance to individual entities, while micro-oriented tools set the fundamental rules for system operations.
Micro-oriented tools give operational guidance to entities, while framework policies set fundamental rules that have changed little in recent years.
Both parts deal only with network and system operations, because digital resilience covers the technological but not the financial side.
Micro-oriented tools give general operational guidance, while framework policies set the fundamental rules and have been revised substantially.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the two layers**

Micro-oriented tools deal with general operational guidance. Framework policies deal with the fundamental rules for network and system operations.

**Step 2 – What has happened to them**

Because of the significant threats to digital resilience in recent years, framework policies have seen major revisions to strengthen defences against new cyber and ICT risks.

⇒ Guidance at one level, rules at the other, and the rules have been revised.

**Interpretation**

Digital resilience covers both technological and financial aspects, which is why the reading goes on from these two layers to macroprudential tools aimed at the financial system.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023), Digital Resilience and Financial Stability: The Quest for Policy Tools in the Financial Sector; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the two definitions are exchanged.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the second half: framework policies have seen major revisions, not little change.

c.reason: Scope error: digital resilience covers both technological and financial aspects.

questions.question: An oﬀicial at a national cybersecurity agency is reviewing how the country’s many cyber resilience bodies and standards should be organised. Based on the Banco de España paper, which statement is correct?

options.text: Overlapping bodies should be kept, because the redundancy they create is a useful defence when one of the bodies is itself attacked.
Certification and standardisation of solutions are a starting point, and coordination has led to consolidating cybersecurity bodies.
Certification and standardisation should come only after penetration stress testing has shown where each institution’s defences fail.
The ITU is the EU body that runs penetration stress testing of cloud providers, so national bodies should defer to its results.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The starting point**

The ITU covers a wide range of legal, technical and other measures to promote cyber resilience. Because of the complexity involved, certification and standardisation of solutions are needed as a starting point for building cybersecurity defences.

**Step 2 – Organising the bodies**

With so many entities involved, a well-coordinated effort is needed to maximise eﬀiciency and minimise redundancy. The result has been the consolidation of numerous cybersecurity entities at national level.

⇒ Standardise first; consolidate the bodies.

**Interpretation**

Both points are about coherence: common standards and fewer, better-coordinated bodies. Neither is yet a macroprudential tool; they are the groundwork.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the reading seeks to minimise redundancy, and the trend is consolidation.

c.reason: Sequence error: certification and standardisation are the starting point, not a step that follows testing.

d.reason: Role misassignment: penetration stress testing is a DORA provision; the ITU is cited for its wide range of legal, technical and other measures.

questions.question: A macroprudential supervisor argues that recent forward-looking, principles-based operational resilience rules are enough on their own to contain systemic cyber risk. Which response best reflects the Banco de España paper?

options.text: The premise is wrong: recent operational resilience rules are more prescriptive and backward-looking than the rules they replaced.
The supervisor is right, because a principles-based approach is at its most useful when a risk spans many entities at once.
The supervisor is wrong: principles-based rules suit one entity’s risk better than systemic risk, which spans multiple entities.
The supervisor is right, because the rules replaced tick-the-box compliance with judgment, which removes the need for other tools.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Grant the premise**

Recent operational resilience rules are indeed more forward-looking and principles-based than past rules, which they need to be to evolve with the growing complexity of cyber resilience.

**Step 2 – The caveat**

A principles-based approach is more useful when working with the risk of a given entity than with systemic risk, which involves multiple entities.

⇒ Entity-level principles do not by themselves contain a system-wide risk.

**Interpretation**

This is the bridge from the policy measures to the macroprudential tools: the systemic part of cyber risk needs instruments that act across institutions.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: recent rules are more forward-looking and principles-based, not more prescriptive and backward-looking.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the caveat: principles-based rules are more useful for a given entity than for risk spanning many entities.

d.reason: Sibling swap with overreach: the move from tick-the-box compliance to a judgment-based system is the reading’s point about cooperation in the United States, and nothing in the reading says it removes the need for other tools.

questions.question: The head of compliance at a Dutch bank is mapping EU initiatives on digital resilience for the board. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ESRB has proposed EU-wide coordination of incident reporting; DORA covers ICT third-party risks from cloud computing.
DORA has proposed EU-wide coordination of incident reporting; the ESRB runs penetration stress tests of EU banks.
The EU has only recently begun incident reporting and information sharing, under the ESRB’s proposal for a European-wide structure.
DORA covers penetration stress testing but leaves ICT third-party risks from cloud computing to Sheltered Harbor-type arrangements.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The ESRB**

Policies for incident reporting and information sharing have long been in place in the EU. Going a step further, the European Systemic Risk Board has suggested forming a European-wide structure for coordinating incident reporting.

**Step 2 – DORA**

The Digital Operational Resilience Act has provisions to respond to ICT third-party risks associated with cloud computing, and provisions on penetration stress testing.

⇒ ESRB: coordinated reporting. DORA: cloud third-party risk and penetration testing.

**Interpretation**

Attribution questions turn on who did what. Keep the four names apart: ITU (certification and standardisation), ESRB (incident reporting structure), DORA (cloud third-party risk, penetration testing), Sheltered Harbor (US ICT buffer).

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.4)

b.reason: Role misassignment: the two bodies’ roles are swapped. The ESRB made the incident reporting proposal; penetration testing sits in DORA.

c.reason: Polarity flip on timing: EU incident reporting and information sharing policies have long been in place; the ESRB proposal goes a step further.

d.reason: Role misassignment and jurisdiction error: DORA covers ICT third-party risks from cloud computing, and Sheltered Harbor is a US arrangement among banks.

questions.question: A deposit insurer’s policy team is evaluating circuit breakers as a response to a major cyber incident at a bank. Which statement about circuit breakers is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: They are a long-term suspension of normal rules and regulations, giving the bank as much time as it needs to rebuild its systems.
They are a temporary pause on normal rules that supplements deposit controls and targets the run a loss of confidence brings.
They are a valid substitute for existing deposit controls, because a pause in normal rules makes those controls unnecessary.
They have been used extensively in banking for many decades, so the paper treats them as a long-proven tool for cyber incidents.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What it is**

A circuit breaker is a temporary pause on normal rules and regulations, analogous to a temporary stoppage to analyse the fallout from a major attack and decide the next steps for recovery.

**Step 2 – What it is for**

After a major cyber incident, it minimises the negative impact of customers’ loss of confidence and the resulting bank run on deposits. It supplements the controls already in place for deposits.

⇒ Temporary, targeted at the run, added to existing controls.

**Interpretation**

The circuit breaker is the macroprudential answer to the end point of CI-8 b: the loss of confidence that turns into a run.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q84 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip on duration: the pause is temporary.

c.reason: Sibling swap: circuit breakers supplement deposit controls; they are not a substitute.

d.reason: Timeline error: circuit breakers have been used more in the banking industry in recent years, not extensively for decades.

questions.question: The general counsel of a bank hit by a severe cyberattack is preparing the bank’s request to its supervisor to activate a circuit breaker. Which challenge to the adoption of this tool does the Banco de España paper identify?

options.text: The supervisor must prove the attack is serious enough to be force majeure, because pausing normal rules is the supervisor’s decision.
It works only once standardisation and thorough incident reporting have been brought to an international level, which has not yet happened.
The pause weakens stewardship over the bank’s operations, because normal rules and oversight are suspended while it lasts.
The bank must prove the attack is serious enough to be force majeure, against the argument that proper controls could have avoided it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The burden on the bank**

The challenge is for the bank to prove that the attack is serious enough to be considered a force majeure event, which would give it some recovery time.

**Step 2 – The counter-argument**

It could be argued that proper cyber controls and other preventative measures could have avoided the negative effects, so the attack is not force majeure.

**Step 3 – The case for**

Circuit breakers can control and minimise the negative effects of a potential bank run after a significant attack.

⇒ The diﬀiculty is the trigger, not the usefulness of the tool.

**Interpretation**

The burden of proof sits with the bank, and the obstacle is the preventability argument. The other options either move that burden or borrow a challenge or cost that the reading attaches to something else; learn the shaded column of Figure 2 row by row.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.a and LO 107.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q87 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (completion box) (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.6)

a.reason: Role misassignment: the reading puts the burden on the bank, which must prove the attack is serious enough to be force majeure; the supervisor does not have to prove it.

b.reason: Sibling swap: bringing standardisation and thorough reporting to an international level is the challenge for cooperative arrangements.

c.reason: Sibling swap: weaker stewardship is the unintended cost of multiclouds (CI-8 a), not of a circuit breaker, whose stated challenge is the force majeure test.

questions.question: A US bank’s board is asked to join Sheltered Harbor, LLC. Under the arrangement, if a co-owner bank suffers a serious cyberattack, its customers can transact on their accounts at another co-owner bank, supported by consistent data formats and procedures for storing and restoring data. How does the Banco de España paper classify this tool?

options.text: As a cooperative arrangement: an ICT buffer that allows a much quicker recovery for a co-owner bank hit by a major cyberattack.
As a circuit breaker: a temporary pause on normal rules that limits the deposit run after the attacked bank loses customer confidence.
As a structural measure: forced diversification that requires each bank to spread its customers’ accounts across several providers.
As a micro-oriented tool: general operational guidance on data storage and restoration that each co-owner bank applies on its own.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the mechanism**

Customers of an attacked co-owner bank transact on their accounts at another co-owner bank, with consistent data formats and operating procedures for storing and restoring data.

**Step 2 – Classify it**

This is an ICT buffer, which the reading gives as a good example of cooperation against systemic risk. It allows a much quicker recovery for a bank that has suffered a major cyberattack. (ICT buffers have also been used in the past in the US tri-party repo system.)

⇒ A cooperative arrangement.

**Interpretation**

The value of the arrangement is shared: each co-owner bank’s risk from a cyberattack is substantially reduced, because the others stand ready to serve its customers on a common data standard.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q83 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap: a circuit breaker pauses normal rules; Sheltered Harbor keeps customers transacting through another bank.

c.reason: Sibling swap: forced diversification pushes firms toward multiclouds or multiple types of software. Nothing in Sheltered Harbor spreads accounts across providers.

d.reason: Layer swap: micro-oriented tools are general operational guidance. The common data formats here serve an arrangement that works across co-owner banks against systemic risk; no bank applies it on its own.

questions.question: A senior oﬀicial at an international standard-setting body is reviewing progress on cooperation against cyber threats in the financial sector. Which statement is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: Cooperation came quickly in finance, because most financial organisations are small or medium-sized and gain most from sharing resources.
The United States has moved from judgment-based cybersecurity standards to tick-the-box compliance, which eases international comparison.
The US has moved toward unified, judgment-based standards; the remaining challenge is international standardisation and reporting.
Cooperation on incident reporting has declined in Europe and internationally as authorities consolidate around national bodies.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Progress**

In the United States there has been progress in unifying the various cybersecurity standards and in moving from tick-the-box compliance to a judgment-based system.

**Step 2 – The challenge**

The challenge remains to bring standardisation and thorough reporting to an international level, although cooperation on incident reporting has been rising in Europe and internationally. Option C states both halves: the national progress and the international challenge.

⇒ National progress; the international step is the hard part.

**Interpretation**

Cooperation was also slow to start: it may seem obvious for small and medium-sized organisations, but it took time in a sector where most organisations are large.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip on size: cooperation took time precisely because most financial organisations are large.

b.reason: Polarity flip on direction: the move is from tick-the-box compliance to a judgment-based system.

d.reason: Polarity flip on the trend: cooperation on incident reporting has been rising in Europe and internationally.

questions.question: A regulator proposes penalties for banks that rely on a single software vendor for critical services, to push them toward using multiple types of software. Which assessment is most consistent with the Banco de España paper?

options.text: This is a cooperative arrangement, and its main challenge is proving that a vendor failure is serious enough to be a force majeure event.
This is forced diversification, a structural measure; penalties act as negative motivators but raise the issue of enforceability.
This is a circuit breaker for software concentration, and the paper finds penalties of this kind straightforward to enforce.
This is a structural measure, but the paper rules out penalties and limits regulators to evaluating critical providers more thoroughly.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Classify the proposal**

Pushing firms toward multiclouds or multiple types of software is what the reading calls forced diversification, one of the structural measures.

**Step 2 – The lever and its challenge**

Penalties for concentrated software use could be used as negative motivators; however, penalties introduce the issue of enforceability.

⇒ Right tool for concentration, hard to enforce.

**Interpretation**

The regulator’s other options under structural measures are softer: more thorough evaluations of critical providers, strongly encouraging multicloud services and using private clouds.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.9)

a.reason: Sibling swap twice: the proposal is a structural measure, not a cooperative arrangement, and force majeure is the circuit breaker’s challenge.

c.reason: Sibling swap with a polarity flip: it is not a circuit breaker, and penalties raise the issue of enforceability rather than being straightforward.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the reading says penalties could be used, with an enforceability problem; it does not rule them out.

questions.question: A financial stability committee is discussing the banking sector’s heavy dependence on a handful of large cloud and technology providers. Which recommendation best reflects the Banco de España paper’s discussion of structural measures?

options.text: Leave the providers outside macroprudential regulation, because their externalities fall on technology markets rather than on the financial sector.
Encourage banks to consolidate on the single most robust provider, so that supervisors can concentrate their oversight in one place.
Treat them as SITIs within macroprudential reach or, as alternatives, evaluate critical providers closely and encourage multiclouds.
Bring them within macroprudential reach as SITIs, but discourage multiclouds, which the paper finds add to concentration risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the providers come into scope**

The reach of macroprudential regulation has inevitably spread to systemically important technological institutions (SITIs), given the numerous externalities they create and the financial sector’s significant dependence on them.

**Step 2 – The alternatives**

Alternatives to macroprudential regulation include more thorough evaluations of critical providers, strongly encouraging multicloud services and using private clouds.

⇒ Bring the providers in, or manage the dependence through evaluation and diversification.

**Interpretation**

Encouraging multiclouds answers concentration risk, but it carries the cost named in CI-8 a: weaker stewardship over distributed computing processes. The committee should weigh both.

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.a and LO 107.c

**Source:** Adapted from CI QB Imp Q86 • SchweserNotes Book 5, LO 107.c; CI notes CI-8 c (Current Issues Workbook, Question CI-8 c.10)

a.reason: Polarity flip: macroprudential reach has spread to SITIs, precisely because of their externalities and the financial sector’s dependence on them.

b.reason: Polarity flip: concentrating on one provider is the concentration risk the reading wants reduced through multiclouds.

d.reason: Half right, half reversed: macroprudential reach has spread to SITIs, but multiclouds are the evolution meant to deal with concentration risk, and strongly encouraging them is one of the alternatives.
